by_decile <- prs |>
  mutate(decile = ntile(PRS_z, 10)) |>
  group_by(decile) |>
  summarise(n = n(), cases = sum(disease), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(risk = cases / n,
         OR_vs_middle = (risk / (1 - risk)) /
                        (risk[decile == 5] / (1 - risk[decile == 5])))

ggplot(by_decile, aes(decile, OR_vs_middle)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#185FA5") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  labs(x = "PRS decile", y = "OR vs middle decile",
       title = "Risk by PRS decile — referenced to the middle, not the bottom") +
  theme_minimal()











import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

prs["decile"] = pd.qcut(prs.PRS_z, 10, labels=False) + 1
by_decile = prs.groupby("decile").agg(n=("disease", "size"), cases=("disease", "sum"))
by_decile["risk"] = by_decile.cases / by_decile.n
odds = by_decile.risk / (1 - by_decile.risk)

title: W3. GWAS와 Post-GWAS
text:
노트🎯 학습목표





이 장을 마치면 다음을 할 수 있어야 합니다.

GWAS가 무엇을 묻고 구조적으로 무엇에는 답할 수 없는지 설명한다
형질의 유전적 구조(genetic architecture)를 알아보고, 그것이 연구 설계를 결정하는 이유를 설명한다
⚠️ Manhattan plot보다 QQ plot을 먼저 읽고 λ가 무엇을 말하는지 설명한다
기준값이 5×10⁻⁸인 이유와 “suggestive” 결과의 가치를 설명한다
⚠️ 보고된 lead SNP가 대개 causal variant가 아닌 이유를 설명한다
하나의 hit가 기전 주장에 이르는 네 단계의 post-GWAS 과정을 추적한다
유럽인 GWAS 결과가 한국 환자에게 적용되지 않을 수 있는 이유를 설명한다
10분 안에 자신이 진료하는 질환을 GWAS Catalog와 Open Targets에서 찾아본다

title: W3. GWAS와 Post-GWAS
section: 1) 이미 진료에 영향을 주는 다섯 가지 방식
text:
1) 이미 진료에 영향을 주는 다섯 가지 방식

Drug target validation — 사람의 유전적 근거가 있는 target은 승인까지 살아남을 가능성이 약 두 배 높습니다
Disease subtyping — 같은 ICD code라도 유전적 구조와 생물학이 다를 수 있습니다
Risk stratification — 예방의학에서의 polygenic score(🔗 W4)
Shared aetiology — genetic correlation은 두 진단이 함께 나타나는 이유를 정량화합니다
Causal inference — Mendelian randomization은 RCT를 수행하지 않고 인과성을 검정합니다

💡 최근 Nature Medicine 호를 아무거나 펼쳐보세요. 임상적 주장 아래로 인용을 세 개쯤 따라가면 GWAS 데이터가 나올 가능성이 높습니다.

title: W3. GWAS와 Post-GWAS
text:
2) GWAS가 실제로 묻는 것

“질환 X가 없는 matched control보다 질환 X가 있는 사람에게 더 흔한 genetic variant는 무엇인가?”


수백만 개 variant의 allele frequency를 동시에 비교합니다
Hypothesis-free — 연구자가 어떤 유전자를 중요하게 생각하는지 알지도, 신경 쓰지도 않습니다
출력은 연관된 locus의 목록입니다. ⚠️ Gene도, mechanism도 아닙니다


SNP (single-nucleotide polymorphism)

두 개 이상의 allele이 흔하게 나타나는 염기 하나의 위치(MAF ≥ 1%)입니다. 사람은 약 1,000만 개의 common SNP를 가지며, array는 50만–500만 개를 직접 측정하고 나머지는 reference panel에서 imputation합니다.

대규모 GWAS


Omnigenic
발현되는 거의 모든 유전자
대부분의 complex trait
초대형 GWAS + network









중요Sample size가 운명을 결정하지만, 이것은 비판이 아니다





Schizophrenia GWAS는 n이 수백일 때 사실상 아무것도 찾지 못했지만, n이 수만으로 늘자 108개 locus를 찾았습니다. 생물학은 바뀌지 않았습니다.

⚠️ 초기 GWAS의 “실패” 대부분은 틀린 연구가 아니라 polygenic architecture에 비해 검정력이 부족한 연구였습니다
💡 그래서 환자 200명의 single-centre GWAS는 실행 가능한 project가 아니며, consortium 참여가 이 분야의 실질적인 자산입니다

→ Effect size와 druggability도 서로 무관합니다. Common HMGCR variant가 설명하는 LDL 분산은 약 0.26%에 불과합니다. Statin은 의학에 가장 큰 영향을 준 약물 중 하나입니다.

title: W3. GWAS와 Post-GWAS
text:
1) QQ plot을 먼저 본다
모든 GWAS 논문은 Manhattan plot을 보여줍니다. 정직성은 QQ plot에 있으며, 흔히 supplement에 숨어 있습니다.



왼쪽에서 오른쪽으로 읽으세요. 전체 분포가 이동했습니까, 아니면 꼬리만 들렸습니까?


Genomic inflation factor λ는 관측된 test statistic의 median과 null에서 기대되는 median을 비교합니다.

✅ λ ≈ 1.0이고 꼬리만 들림 — calibration이 잘 되었으며 꼬리의 신호는 실제입니다
❌ λ > 1.05이고 선 전체가 올라감 — 보정되지 않은 population stratification 또는 relatedness입니다. Hit를 의심해야 합니다
⚠️ λ < 0.95 — 지나치게 보수적인 QC로 power를 버렸습니다







노트알아둘 가치가 있는 예외





n이 매우 크면 약한 inflation이 실제 polygenicity일 수 있습니다. 수천 개 variant가 정말로 작은 효과를 가진다면 null이 적절한 비교 대상이 아니기 때문입니다.
✅ LD-score regression은 inflation이 LD score에 따라 증가하는지(polygenicity), 균일한지(confounding)를 확인해 둘을 구분합니다. 현대적인 논문은 λ와 함께 LDSC intercept를 보고합니다. Review에서 이것이 없는 이유를 물어도 좋습니다.

title: W3. GWAS와 Post-GWAS
text:
2) 그다음 Manhattan plot



각 점은 variant이며, 높이는 effect size가 아니라 −log₁₀(p)입니다.


5×10⁻⁸인 이유: LD pruning 뒤에는 독립적인 common-variant test가 약 100만 개 남습니다. Bonferroni를 적용하면 0.05 / 10⁶ = 5×10⁻⁸입니다.

⚠️ 이 threshold는 common SNP에 맞춰져 있습니다. Rare-variant test와 structural-variant test에는 각자의 기준이 필요합니다
⚠️ “Suggestive”(p < 1×10⁻⁵)는 관례일 뿐 발견이 아닙니다. Suggestive-only 결과는 hypothesis로 취급하세요







경고Population stratification — 아름다운 거짓 양성을 만드는 confounder





Case와 control의 ancestry가 체계적으로 다르면 ancestry와 관련된 모든 variant가 disease hit처럼 보입니다. 한국인 case group과 ancestry가 섞인 control group을 비교하면 젓가락 사용에 대한 “hit”를 찾게 됩니다.
✅ 해결책: Genotype으로 계산한 principal component를 covariate에 포함합니다.

RPython



# toy cohort so the model runs (illustration only)
set.seed(1)
n <- 2000
toy <- data.frame(SNP = rbinom(n, 2, 0.3), matrix(rnorm(n * 5), n, 5,
                  dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("PC", 1:5))),
                  age = rnorm(n, 55, 10), sex = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5),
                  batch = factor(sample(1:3, n, replace = TRUE)))
toy$disease <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1 + 0.3 * toy$SNP + 0.5 * toy$PC1))

glm(disease ~ SNP +
      PC1 + PC2 + PC3 + PC4 + PC5 +   # ancestry
      age + sex + batch,              # nuisance
    family = binomial, data = toy)

    sex + batch, family = binomial, data = toy)

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

# toy cohort so the model runs (illustration only)
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 2000
toy = pd.DataFrame(rng.normal(size=(n, 5)), columns=[f"PC{i}" for i in range(1, 6)])
toy["SNP"] = rng.binomial(2, 0.3, n)

toy["disease"] = rng.binomial(1, 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(-1 + 0.3 * toy.SNP + 0.5 * toy.PC1))))

smf.logit("disease ~ SNP"
          " + PC1 + PC2 + PC3 + PC4 + PC5"     # ancestry

text:
3) 그림 전에 수행된 QC

title: W3. GWAS와 Post-GWAS
text:
1) Linkage disequilibrium이 만드는 문제
LD는 측정된 variant 하나로 측정하지 않은 수십 개를 tag하게 하므로 GWAS를 가능하게 합니다. 동시에 tag와 원인이 통계적으로 동일하게 보이게 하므로 해석을 망가뜨립니다.



같은 locus와 같은 생물학이지만 population은 다릅니다.








중요논문을 읽을 때 이것이 뜻하는 것





“질환 X와 연관된 rs1234567을 발견했다”는 문장은 거의 언제나 다음을 뜻합니다.
→ “rs1234567과 약 40개의 다른 variant를 포함하는 haplotype block 어딘가에서 무언가가 어떤 작용을 하고 있다.”

❌ Lead SNP는 이 sample에서 p-value가 가장 작은 variant입니다. 다른 cohort에서 다시 분석하면 이웃 variant가 이기는 경우가 흔합니다
⚠️ Fine-mapping 없이 lead SNP 자체의 생물학을 논하는 논문은 자신의 데이터를 과도하게 해석하는 것입니다
✅ 올바른 표현은 “locus”이며 현대적인 논문은 이 용어를 사용합니다

title: W3. GWAS와 Post-GWAS
text:
2) 우편번호에서 기전까지의 네 단계



각 단계는 주장의 범위를 좁힙니다. 하나를 건너뛰면 reviewer가 찾아낼 틈이 남습니다.


① Fine-mapping. Bayesian method(SuSiE, FINEMAP)는 각 variant에 posterior inclusion probability를 부여하고, 예를 들어 causal variant를 95% 확률로 포함하는 가장 작은 집합인 credible set을 반환합니다.

💡 Credible set이 3개라는 것은 결과입니다. 40개라는 것은 해소하지 못했다는 고백입니다
⚠️ Ancestry-matched LD reference가 필요합니다. 유럽인 panel을 한국인 cohort에 적용하면 출력이 조용히 손상됩니다
⚠️ PIP가 많은 variant에 얇게 분산된다면 정직한 결론은 “이 sample에서는 이 locus를 해소할 수 없다”입니다

② Functional annotation. Variant가 어디에 위치합니까?







위치
가능성 높은 mechanism




Coding (missense, nonsense)
직접적인 protein 변화


Splice site
달라진 mRNA 또는 isoform


Promoter / 5′UTR
transcription 조절


Enhancer
멀리 떨어진 gene의 조절일 수 있음


Intergenic / intronic
⚠️ 알 수 없음 — eQTL과 chromatin data 필요



⚠️ GWAS hit의 약 90%는 non-coding입니다. 이 사실 하나가 이 수업의 나머지 부분이 필요한 이유입니다.
③ Variant → gene. eQTL은 gene expression에 영향을 주는 variant입니다. Colocalisation은 GWAS와 eQTL signal이 동일한 causal variant를 공유하는지 묻습니다.

RPython



library(coloc)

# toy locus: 200 variants, variant 100 drives both signals (illustration only)
set.seed(2)
maf    <- runif(200, 0.05, 0.5)
causal <- seq_len(200) == 100
gwas_p <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(rnorm(200) + 8 * causal))
eqtl_p <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(rnorm(200) + 6 * causal))

snp    <- paste0("v", 1:200)

res <- coloc.abf(
  dataset1 = list(pvalues = gwas_p, N = 150000, type = "cc", s = 0.3, MAF = maf, snp = snp),
  dataset2 = list(pvalues = eqtl_p, N = 500,    type = "quant",      MAF = maf, snp = snp)
)
res$summary["PP.H4.abf"]   # > 0.8 → they share a causal variant

PP.H0.abf PP.H1.abf PP.H2.abf PP.H3.abf PP.H4.abf 
 7.94e-14  9.21e-08  8.62e-10  1.51e-09  1.00e+00 
[1] "PP abf for shared variant: 100%"
PP.H4.abf 
0.9999999 





import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm
from scipy.special import logsumexp

# toy locus: 200 variants, variant 100 drives both signals (illustration only)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
maf    = rng.uniform(0.05, 0.5, 200)
causal = np.arange(1, 201) == 100
gwas_p = 2 * norm.sf(np.abs(rng.normal(size=200) + 8 * causal))
eqtl_p = 2 * norm.sf(np.abs(rng.normal(size=200) + 6 * causal))

# coloc.abf written out (Wakefield approximate Bayes factors, coloc's default priors)
def log_abf(p, maf, N, s=None, sd_prior=0.15):
    z2 = norm.isf(p / 2) ** 2
    V = 1 / (2 * N * maf * (1 - maf))
    if s is not None:                              # case-control: scale by s(1-s), prior sd 0.2
        V, sd_prior = V / (s * (1 - s)), 0.2
    r = sd_prior**2 / (sd_prior**2 + V)
    return 0.5 * (np.log(1 - r) + r * z2)

l1 = log_abf(gwas_p, maf, 150000, s=0.3)
l2 = log_abf(eqtl_p, maf, 500)
p1, p2, p12 = 1e-4, 1e-4, 1e-5
lH = np.array([
    0,
    np.log(p1) + logsumexp(l1),
    np.log(p2) + logsumexp(l2),
    np.log(p1) + np.log(p2) + logsumexp([logsumexp(l1) + logsumexp(l2), logsumexp(l1 + l2)], b=[1, -1]),
    np.log(p12) + logsumexp(l1 + l2),
])
pp = np.exp(lH - logsumexp(lH))
print("PP.H4.abf =", round(pp[4], 3))   # > 0.8 → they share a causal variant

PP.H4.abf = 0.999






❌ 가장 가까운 gene은 약 절반의 경우 틀립니다. Enhancer는 가까운 이웃을 건너뛰는 일이 흔합니다
⚠️ 방향을 확인하세요. Risk allele이 환자에서 증가해 보이는 gene을 오히려 down-regulation할 수 있습니다. 이런 불일치는 손상된 보호 반응을 반영하는 경우가 많고 agonist와 antagonist 중 무엇을 선택할지 결정합니다

④ Gene → cell type. Colocalisation은 gene을 알려줄 뿐 위치를 알려주지 않습니다. sc-linker 같은 framework는 stratified LD-score regression을 통해 single-cell data와 GWAS를 결합하여 Alzheimer disease에서는 microglia, eczema에서는 T cell을 찾아냅니다. 🔗 W5에서 다시 다룹니다.
⑤ Causality. Mendelian randomization은 variant를 instrument로 사용합니다. Variant는 수정 시점에 무작위로 배정되므로 lifestyle confounding에 영향을 받지 않는 평생의 RCT를 모방합니다.
Genetic variants  →  LDL level  →  CAD
   (instrument)      (exposure)   (outcome)
⚠️ 세 가지 IV assumption은 relevance, instrument에 대한 confounding 부재, exclusion restriction입니다. 세 번째는 pleiotropy 때문에 깨집니다. MR-Egger와 weighted median은 바로 이것을 확인하기 위해 존재합니다. 단일 방법만 사용한 MR 결과는 불완전합니다.

title: W3. GWAS와 Post-GWAS
text:
1) GWAS Catalog — 무엇이 알려져 있는가?
ebi.ac.uk/gwas → 질환을 검색합니다.

① 보고된 association은 몇 개입니까? 연구는 몇 개입니까?
② 가장 큰 연구를 클릭하세요. Sample size와 ancestry는 무엇입니까?
③ 보고된 variant를 보세요. Gene label이 붙은 것은 몇 개이며 intergenic은 몇 개입니까?
④ ⚠️ 이 질환을 대상으로 한 동아시아 연구가 하나라도 있습니까? 유럽 연구와 비교해 n은 얼마입니까?

title: W3. GWAS와 Post-GWAS
text:
2) Open Targets — 약물이 있는가?
platform.opentargets.org → 질환 → target list로 이동합니다.

⑤ 가장 점수가 높은 target은 무엇이며, 어떤 evidence type이 뒷받침합니까? (genetic, expression, literature, animal model)
⑥ 이 target을 대상으로 승인되었거나 임상시험 중인 약물이 있습니까? 어떤 indication입니까?
⑦ 💡 강한 genetic evidence가 있지만 약물이 없는 target을 찾으세요. 이미 justification paragraph가 갖춰진 연구 질문입니다

title: W3. GWAS와 Post-GWAS
text:
3) 모든 locus를 조사하는 checklist
Journal club에서 사용할 수 있도록 보관하세요.

① 독립된 cohort에서 replication되었습니까?
② Credible set이 얼마나 큽니까? 아니면 fine-mapping을 건너뛰었습니까?
③ Coding, regulatory, unknown 중 무엇입니까? eQTL이 있습니까?
④ 어떤 gene, 어떤 cell type입니까? Nearest ≠ causal임을 기억하세요
⑤ Effect size와 방향 — 방향이 drug strategy를 결정합니다
⑥ 어떤 ancestry이며 실제 적용할 환자와 일치합니까?

title: W3. GWAS와 Post-GWAS
text:
4) Summary statistic을 직접 다뤄보고 싶다면
공개 summary statistic은 variant마다 한 행이 있고 개인 genotype은 포함하지 않으므로 자유롭게 공유할 수 있습니다. §7.1에서 고른 연구를 내려받으세요. scripts/download_public_data.R이 제각각인 column name을 정리합니다.

RPython



library(tidyverse); library(qqman); library(here)

gwas <- read_tsv(here("rawdata", "t2d_gwas_summary.tsv"))

clean <- gwas |> filter(!is.na(P), P > 0, P <= 1, FREQ > 0.01, FREQ < 0.99)

# λ first, always
lambda <- function(p) {
  chisq <- qchisq(p, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
  median(chisq) / qchisq(0.5, df = 1)
}
cat("lambda =", round(lambda(clean$P), 3), "\n")

qq(clean$P, main = paste0("QQ — λ = ", round(lambda(clean$P), 3)), col = "#185FA5")

manhattan(clean, chr = "CHR", bp = "BP", p = "P", snp = "SNP",
          col = c("#185FA5", "#9db8d1"),
          suggestiveline = -log10(1e-5), genomewideline = -log10(5e-8))

lambda = 1.302 



















import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import chi2

gwas = pd.read_csv("rawdata/t2d_gwas_summary.tsv", sep="\t")

clean = gwas.query("P > 0 and P <= 1 and FREQ > 0.01 and FREQ < 0.99")

# λ first, always
def lam(p):
    return np.median(chi2.isf(p, 1)) / chi2.ppf(0.5, 1)
print("lambda =", round(lam(clean.P), 3))

# QQ plot
n = len(clean)
expected = -np.log10((np.arange(1, n + 1) - 0.5) / n)
observed = -np.log10(np.sort(clean.P.to_numpy()))
plt.scatter(expected, observed, s=2, c="#185FA5")
plt.axline((0, 0), slope=1, c="red")
plt.title(f"QQ — λ = {lam(clean.P):.3f}")
plt.xlabel("Expected -log10(p)"); plt.ylabel("Observed -log10(p)")
plt.show()

# Manhattan plot
d = clean.sort_values(["CHR", "BP"])
offset = d.groupby("CHR").BP.max().cumsum().shift(fill_value=0)
x = d.BP + d.CHR.map(offset)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 4))
ax.scatter(x, -np.log10(d.P), s=2, c=np.where(d.CHR % 2, "#185FA5", "#9db8d1"))
ax.axhline(-np.log10(1e-5), c="blue", lw=0.8)
ax.axhline(-np.log10(5e-8), c="red", lw=0.8)
ticks = x.groupby(d.CHR).median()
ax.set_xticks(ticks, ticks.index)
ax.set_xlabel("Chromosome"); ax.set_ylabel("-log10(p)")
plt.show()

lambda = 1.302



















✅ 세 가지를 바꾸고, 매번 λ가 어떻게 움직이는지 보세요.

RPython



# ① Drop the MHC — one enormous, hyper-polymorphic locus on chr6
no_mhc <- clean |> filter(!(CHR == 6 & BP > 25e6 & BP < 34e6))
cat("without MHC :", round(lambda(no_mhc$P), 3), "\n")

# ② Common variants only — rarer variants are noisier and less well imputed
common <- clean |> filter(FREQ > 0.05, FREQ < 0.95)
cat("MAF > 5%    :", round(lambda(common$P), 3), "\n")

# ③ ⚠️ λ scales with sample size. Rescale to a notional n = 1000 per group
#    so it can be compared across studies at all
n_eff  <- median(clean$N, na.rm = TRUE)
cat("lambda_1000 :", round(1 + (lambda(clean$P) - 1) * 1000 / n_eff, 4), "\n")

without MHC : 1.294 
MAF > 5%    : 1.39 
lambda_1000 : 1.0007 





# ① Drop the MHC — one enormous, hyper-polymorphic locus on chr6
no_mhc = clean.query("not (CHR == 6 and BP > 25e6 and BP < 34e6)")
print("without MHC :", round(lam(no_mhc.P), 3))

# ② Common variants only — rarer variants are noisier and less well imputed
common = clean.query("FREQ > 0.05 and FREQ < 0.95")
print("MAF > 5%    :", round(lam(common.P), 3))

# ③ ⚠️ λ scales with sample size. Rescale to a notional n = 1000 per group
#    so it can be compared across studies at all
n_eff = clean.N.median()
print("lambda_1000 :", round(1 + (lam(clean.P) - 1) * 1000 / n_eff, 4))

without MHC : 1.294
MAF > 5%    : 1.39
lambda_1000 : 1.0007





💡 ③을 기억할 가치가 있습니다. 대규모 biobank GWAS는 실제 polygenicity 때문에 λ가 n과 함께 커져 λ = 1.15여도 calibration이 완벽할 수 있습니다. λ₁₀₀₀을 사용해야 두 연구를 비교할 수 있습니다. 논문에 이 값이 없다면 이유를 물어도 좋습니다.

3) 이름이 있는 section
Comment 끝에 dash 네 개를 붙이면 이동 가능한 section이 됩니다(⌘/Ctrl + Shift + R로 삽입).

# Libraries ----
library(DESeq2)

# Load ----
dds <- readRDS(here("analysis", "1_clean.rds"))

# Filter — 3 samples excluded, RIN < 6 ----
dds <- dds[, dds$RIN >= 6]

# Test ----
dds <- DESeq(dds)

✅ Section은 RStudio의 outline pane에 나타납니다. ✅ 세 번째 section에 주목하세요. 결정의 이유가 section 제목 안에 있으므로 코드와 떨어질 수 없습니다.

text:
4) 함수 — 언제 만들 것인가
규칙은 “항상 함수를 작성하라”가 아닙니다. 세 번째로 copy-paste할 때 멈추라는 것입니다.

# The pattern that goes wrong — copy-paste per cell type
cd8 <- FindMarkers(seurat, ident.1 = "CD8 T", min.pct = 0.25)
cd4 <- FindMarkers(seurat, ident.1 = "CD4 T", min.pct = 0.25)
nk  <- FindMarkers(seurat, ident.1 = "NK",    min.pct = 0.5)   # ⚠️ typo, or intentional?

# Write it once
get_markers <- function(obj, cell_type, min_pct = 0.25) {
  FindMarkers(obj, ident.1 = cell_type, min.pct = min_pct) |>
    as_tibble(rownames = "gene") |>
    mutate(cell_type = cell_type)
}

all_markers <- map_dfr(c("CD8 T", "CD4 T", "NK"), \(x) get_markers(seurat, x))

⚠️ 목적은 코드의 우아함이 아닙니다. Copy-paste한 버전에서는 세 번째 줄의 min.pct = 0.5가 눈에 띄지 않지만, “NK marker”의 의미를 조용히 바꿉니다.

1) 실제로 달라진 것
자연어로 원하는 것을 설명하고 결과를 반복해서 개선하는 vibe coding은 2025년에 주류 작업 방식이 되었습니다. 임상의에게는 실제 장벽 하나를 없애줍니다. 질문에서 흥미로운 부분은 애초에 문법이 아니었기 때문입니다.







실제로 없앤 것

text:
2) 작동하는 prompt
세 가지 요소가 필요합니다. Context, task, constraints입니다.
Context: `cell_type`에 세포 유형이, `condition`에 질병 상태가
         저장된 Seurat object `seurat`가 있다(level: "IBD", "control").
         샘플 식별자는 `sample_id`에 있으며 donor는 총 12명이다.

Task:    세포 유형 이름을 받아 donor별로 count를 aggregate하고,
         gene symbol을 포함한 DESeq2 result tibble을 반환하는
         pseudobulk differential expression 함수를 작성하라.

Constraints: dplyr + DESeq2 + here를 사용하라. padj 순으로 정렬한
             tibble을 반환하라. Design choice가 필요한 단계에는
             모두 comment를 달아라.
❌ "write code for my analysis"와 비교해 보세요. 실행은 되지만 다른 질문에 답하는 코드를 얻게 됩니다.
💡 마지막 constraints 줄은 매번 추가할 가치가 있습니다. Model이 자신의 design choice를 표시하게 하면 여러분이 그 결정을 볼 수 있습니다.

text:
3) ⚠️ Verification gate



이 수업의 모든 내용은 ③ 단계가 실제로 수행되는지에 달려 있습니다.








중요“실행되었다”는 사실이 근거로서 무가치한 이유





전통적인 coding error는 요란합니다. 스크립트가 멈춥니다. 그래서 한 세대 전체가 “error가 없음”을 “정답”으로 여기도록 학습되었습니다.
생성된 코드는 이 관계를 뒤집습니다. 유창하고 관용적이며, 대개 문법적으로 완벽합니다. 틀렸을 때는 의미적으로 틀립니다. 즉, 일관된 무언가를 수행하지만 여러분이 요청한 것을 수행하지 않습니다.

❌ Crash는 선물입니다. 어디를 살펴봐야 하는지 정확히 알려줍니다
⚠️ 그럴듯하고 차원까지 맞는 data frame이 위험한 결과입니다

→ 검증 질문은 “실행되었는가?”일 수 없습니다. “출력의 형태와 크기가 내가 예상한 것인가?”여야 합니다. 그러려면 먼저 기대값을 만들어 두어야 합니다.

text:
2) 최소한으로 배우는 Quarto
.qmd 파일은 실행 가능한 code block을 포함한 글입니다. Render하면 HTML, PDF 또는 Word가 됩니다.
---
title: "IBD biopsy cohort — DE analysis"
format: html
---

## Results

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(tidyverse)
res <- readRDS(here::here("analysis", "2_dds.rds"))
sig <- res |> filter(padj < 0.05)
```

차등 발현 유전자(FDR < 0.05)는 `r nrow(sig)`개였으며,
그중 `r sum(sig$log2FoldChange > 0)`개가 증가했습니다.
quarto render report.qmd --to html
quarto render report.qmd --to docx     # for the co-author who wants Word
✅ Inline code r nrow(sig)가 핵심입니다. 문장 속 숫자를 직접 입력하지 않고 계산합니다. 데이터가 바뀌면 다시 render해도 문장은 여전히 참입니다.






노트유용한 chunk option





Chunk 맨 위에 hash와 pipe가 붙은 comment로 작성합니다.







Option
효과




echo: false
코드는 실행하지만 숨김 — 임상 독자를 위한 보고서에 사용


eval: false
코드는 보여주지만 실행하지 않음 — 교육 자료에 사용


warning: false
Package message를 숨김


fig-cap: "..."
Caption을 붙여 그림이 의미와 함께 이동하게 함


cache: true
Render할 때 느린 chunk를 다시 실행하지 않음



💡 이 수업 사이트는 Quarto project입니다. 지금 읽고 있는 모든 페이지가 .qmd 파일입니다.

text:
2) 다섯 가지 명령

# once per machine
git config --global user.name  "Eunji Ha"
git config --global user.email "you@knu.ac.kr"

# once per project
git init

# after each working session — these three, forever
git add .
git commit -m "Add DESeq2 analysis; exclude 3 low-RIN samples"
git push

⚠️ 환자 데이터는 절대 commit하지 마세요. 첫 commit 전에 rawdata/를 .gitignore에 넣습니다.
rawdata/
*.rds
.Rhistory
.Rproj.user/
renv/library/






경고History에 한 번 들어가면 history에 남는다





나중 commit에서 파일을 삭제해도 repository에서 없어지지 않습니다. 이전 version을 복구할 수 있으며, public repository라면 여전히 공개된 상태입니다.
✅ 먼저 .gitignore에 추가하고, 그다음 git init, 그다음 commit합니다. 이 순서를 지키세요.
⚠️ 식별 가능한 데이터를 public repository에 이미 push했다면 정보 공개 사고로 취급하고 IRB와 상의하세요. History rewrite만으로는 충분하지 않습니다.

오류 없이 실행되지만 §2.4에서 설명한 유형의 오류 하나가 숨겨진 30줄짜리 스크립트를 드립니다. 어느 줄인지 알려주지 않은 상태에서 오류를 찾아야 합니다.

# Insert shape checks between every step, then read the numbers
cat("rows before join:", nrow(clin), "\n")
merged <- left_join(clin, expr, by = "sample_id")

W3 — GWAS와 post-GWAS. 설치할 것은 없습니다. 브라우저에서 시작합니다.
실제로 진료하는 질환 하나를 생각해 오세요. GWAS Catalog와 Open Targets에서 함께 찾아봅니다.

title: W1. 소개와 로드맵
text:
노트🎯 학습목표





이 장을 마치면 다음을 할 수 있어야 합니다.

지난 학기의 bulk RNA-seq이 무엇에 답했고, 구조적으로 무엇에는 답할 수 없었는지 설명한다
⚠️ 실행의 깊이(execution depth)와 판단의 깊이(judgment depth)를 구분하고, 이 수업이 어느 쪽을 다루는지 설명한다
하나의 임상 질문이 한 학기 동안 여덟 가지 오믹스 층을 거쳐가는 과정을 추적한다
⚠️ 연구 설계 실수를 되돌릴 수 없게 되는 시점을 짚어낸다
샘플 배치만 보고 batch–group confounding을 알아본다
Fresh, frozen, FFPE 검체로 할 수 있는 것과 할 수 없는 것을 설명한다
3년 뒤에도 실행되는 R 프로젝트를 구성한다

title: W1. 소개와 로드맵
text:
1) 지난 학기에 실제로 얻은 것
조직에서 카운트 데이터를 얻고 순위가 매겨진 유전자 목록을 만들 수 있습니다. 이것은 실제 역량이며, 대부분의 임상의는 갖고 있지 않습니다.
하지만 이것은 혼합물에 대한 한 번의 측정이기도 합니다. 정확히 하나의 질문, 즉 두 조직 집단 사이에서 평균적으로 어떤 유전자가 다른가?에 답합니다.



이 수업의 남은 모든 주차는 같은 유전자 목록을 서로 다른 방향에서 살펴봅니다.


💡 오른쪽의 여섯 질문은 왼쪽 분석의 통계를 개선해도 답할 수 없다는 점에 주목하세요. 이 질문에는 다른 데이터가 필요합니다.

title: W1. 소개와 로드맵
text:
2) 다섯 단계는 달라지지 않았다
유전형, 염색질, 단일세포, peptide 등 기술이 무엇이든 pipeline의 모양은 이미 알고 있는 것과 같습니다.
① Quality control     → 이 데이터를 사용할 수 있는가?
② Alignment /          → 각 측정값은 어디에서 왔고,
   quantification         얼마나 존재하는가?
③ Normalization       → 샘플을 서로 비교할 수 있게 만들기
④ Statistical testing → 어떤 차이가 잡음보다 큰가?
⑤ Interpretation      → 생물학적으로 무엇을 의미하는가?






중요모든 단계가 똑같이 위험한 것은 아니다






① ② 단계는 요란하게 실패합니다. Pipeline이 멈추거나 숫자가 터무니없습니다.
③ ④ 단계는 조용히 실패합니다. Adjusted p-value로 정렬된 847개 유전자의 단정한 표가 나오지만, 겉모습만으로는 잘못되었다는 것을 알 수 없습니다.

⚠️ 계산 분석에 고유한 실패 방식은 분석이 언제나 답을 내놓는다는 것입니다. 실패한 PCR은 빈 gel을 보여주지만, 실패한 분석은 그림을 보여줍니다.

title: W1. 소개와 로드맵
text:
3) ⚠️ 두 가지 깊이
“고급 생물정보학”은 서로 매우 다른 두 가지를 뜻할 수 있습니다. 이 수업은 그중 하나에 집중합니다.



왼쪽 열은 전업으로 해야 하는 일입니다. 오른쪽 열은 여러분만이 갖출 수 있는 역량입니다.








힌트오른쪽 열이 분석가가 아니라 여러분의 몫인 이유





분석가는 pseudobulk model이 수렴했다고 말할 수 있습니다. 하지만 “감소한” 세포 유형이 염증 조직을 dissociation할 때 살아남지 못하는 바로 그 세포인지 말할 수는 없습니다. 분석가는 그 조직을 직접 다뤄본 적이 없기 때문입니다.

✅ 여러분은 검체가 어떤 과정을 거쳤는지, 환자들이 어떤 약물을 사용했는지, 진단이 실제로 무엇을 뜻하는지 압니다
✅ 여러분은 절대위험 2% 차이가 진료를 바꾸는지 압니다
❌ 그 누구도 이 지식을 대신 제공할 수 없으며, 어떤 방법도 그 부재를 보상하지 못합니다

→ 이 수업이 메우려는 것은 코딩 격차가 아닙니다. 올바른 질문을 하고 잘못된 답을 알아볼 만큼의 어휘 격차(vocabulary gap)입니다.

title: W1. 소개와 로드맵
section: 1) 하나의 임상 질문, 여덟 개의 층
text:
1) 하나의 임상 질문, 여덟 개의 층
이 학기는 여러 기법을 구경하는 시간이 아닙니다. 하나의 질문을 실제로 검증할 수 있는 수준에 이를 때까지 아래로 파고드는 과정입니다.



각 층은 그 위의 층이 답하지 못한 질문에 답합니다.


💡 오른쪽 열을 위에서 아래로 읽어보세요. 40개 locus에서 출발해, 특정 조직 위치의 특정 세포 유형에 있는 하나의 유전자와 하나의 후보 약물에 이르기까지 답이 매 단계 더 좁고 실행 가능해진다는 점에 주목하세요.
⚠️ W9–W10의 protein은 증가하지만 mRNA는 그대로라는 행도 보세요. 논문이 인정하는 것보다 여러 층은 더 자주 불일치하며, 대개 그 불일치가 가장 유익한 정보입니다.

title: W1. 소개와 로드맵
text:
3) 12월에 할 수 있어야 하는 것

✅ Methods section을 읽고, 조용히 생략된 내용까지 포함해 실제로 무엇을 했는지 말할 수 있다
✅ 새 데이터를 만들기 위한 연구비를 신청하기 전에 공개 데이터가 이미 질문에 답하는지 찾아볼 수 있다
✅ 연구 설계 회의에서 되돌릴 수 없는 실수를 막을 수 있다
✅ 출판된 결과가 한국 환자에게 재현되지 않을 수 있는 이유를 설명할 수 있다
✅ 마지막 수업에서 데이터로 뒷받침된 연구 제안서를 발표할 수 있다







노트이 수업이 의도적으로 약속하지 않는 것





❌ 도움 없이 spatial deconvolution pipeline을 실행할 수 있게 되는 것.
충분히 바랄 만한 목표이지만, 임상 업무와 병행하는 14회의 2시간 수업으로 달성할 수는 없습니다. 가능하다고 약속하는 사람은 무언가를 팔고 있는 것입니다.
→ 달성 가능한 목표는 자신의 이름이 들어갈 분석을 평가하지 못하는 사람이 되지 않는 것입니다.

title: W1. 소개와 로드맵
text:
1) ⚠️ 시점의 문제



되돌릴 수 없는 결정은 거의 모두 누군가 R을 열기 전에 이루어집니다.








경고“분석은 나중에 생각하자”가 실제로 치르게 하는 비용





실제 연구에서 반복되는 세 가지 상황입니다.

① “그룹당 n = 3이면 충분한가요?” — 검체 수집이 끝난 뒤 묻습니다. 균질한 시스템의 충분한 검정력을 가진 bulk 비교라면 때로는 가능합니다. 조건 간 single-cell 비교에서는 ⚠️ n이 세포 수가 아니라 donor 수이므로(W5), 대개 충분하지 않습니다.
② “조직을 flash-freezing했습니다.” — 그러면 scRNA-seq은 불가능하고 snRNA-seq을 하거나 아무것도 할 수 없습니다(W5). 재앙은 아니지만 주장할 수 있는 내용이 달라집니다.
③ “환자군은 A 병원, 대조군은 B 병원에서 수집했습니다.” — §3.3을 보세요. 해결 방법이 없습니다.

→ 각각은 30초면 예방할 수 있지만, 놓치면 18개월 동안 후회하게 됩니다.

title: W1. 소개와 로드맵
section: 2) 모든 것을 결정하는 세 가지 질문
text:
2) 모든 것을 결정하는 세 가지 질문
검체 하나라도 수집하기 전에 물어야 합니다.
① 내 반복 단위(unit of replication)는 무엇인가?
독립적으로 반복할 수 있는 대상입니다. 보통 환자이며, 세포나 well, technical replicate가 아닙니다.

⚠️ 환자 3명에서 얻은 세포 30,000개는 n = 3입니다
⚠️ 같은 종양을 나눈 두 aliquot은 n = 1입니다

② 정확히 무엇과 무엇을 비교하는가?
수집 전에 문장을 쓰세요. “나는 ___와 ___를 비교하며, ___가 ___ 방향으로 다를 것이라 예상한다.”

❌ “우리 환자를 profiling하고 싶다” — 비교가 아닙니다
✅ “나이와 병기를 matching한 치료 저항군과 치료 경험이 없는 군을 비교한다” — 이제 설계를 도출할 수 있습니다

③ 두 그룹 사이에서 또 무엇이 다른가?
그룹 구분과 함께 달라지는 모든 것은 경쟁 설명입니다. 수집 기관, 보관 기간, sequencing run, 추출일, 작업자, 시간대, 약물이 모두 해당합니다.

title: W1. 소개와 로드맵
text:
3) ⚠️ Batch에 의한 교란



두 배치의 비용은 같지만, 하나만 분석할 수 있습니다.








중요“Batch만 보정하면 된다”가 해결책이 아닌 이유





Batch correction은 같은 batch 안에 있으면서 그룹이 다른 샘플로부터 batch effect를 추정합니다. 두 그룹을 모두 포함하는 batch가 하나도 없다면 추정할 정보가 없습니다.
수학이 까다로운 것이 아닙니다. 필요한 정보가 실제로 데이터에 없습니다. ComBat, limma::removeBatchEffect, Harmony와 그 후속 방법 모두 같은 한계가 있습니다.
✅ 해결책은 비용이 들지 않으며, scheduling의 문제입니다. 모든 run, 모든 추출일, 모든 기관에 두 그룹을 모두 포함하세요.
💡 공동연구자가 이 원칙을 어긴 데이터를 보냈다면 일찍 말해주는 것이 친절입니다. Discussion을 다 쓴 뒤 말하는 것은 그렇지 않습니다.

title: W1. 소개와 로드맵
text:
1) 재현성은 임상 문제다
분석에서 출판까지는 보통 1–3년이 걸립니다. Reviewer가 재분석을 요구하고, package는 업데이트되며, 노트북 컴퓨터가 바뀝니다.
두 가지 습관부터 시작합니다.

프로젝트 기반 작업 — 다시는 setwd()를 사용하지 않기
일관된 디렉터리 구조 — 나와 공동연구자 모두 파일 위치를 알 수 있게 하기

title: W1. 소개와 로드맵
text:
2) R Project (.Rproj)
.Rproj 파일은 자신이 있는 위치를 working directory로 고정합니다.
RStudio → File → New Project → New Directory (or Existing Directory)
확장 가능한 구조:
my_project/
├── my_project.Rproj          ← working directory의 기준점
├── rawdata/                  ← 절대 수정하거나 덮어쓰지 않음
│   └── clinical_data.xlsx
├── scripts/                  ← 실행 순서대로 번호 부여
│   ├── 1_clean.R
│   ├── 2_analysis.R
│   └── 3_figures.R
├── analysis/                 ← 중간 .rds 객체
├── results/
│   ├── figures/
│   └── tables/
└── logs/
💡 번호가 핵심입니다. 2_analysis.R은 1_clean.R보다 먼저 실행할 수 없습니다. 6개월 뒤에는 이 순서가 가장 믿을 만한 문서가 됩니다.

text:
1) 코딩 없이: 내 질문에 이미 답이 있는가?
무언가를 새로 만들기 전에 브라우저에서 20분을 보내세요. 자신의 전문 분야에서 유전자나 질환 하나를 고른 뒤 다음을 차례로 확인합니다.



리소스
질문




GWAS Catalog
이 질환의 variant가 이미 발견되었는가? 몇 개이며, 어떤 집단에서 발견되었는가?


Open Targets
내 유전자는 이미 이 질환과 연결되어 있는가? 관련 약물이 있는가?

CELLxGENE

GEO
누군가 이미 이 실험을 수행하고 데이터를 공개했는가?



✅ 찾은 내용과 계획한 실험이 여전히 새로운 가치를 더하는지를 각각 한 문장으로 적으세요.
💡 단순한 준비운동이 아닙니다. Translational research에서 가장 생산적인 한 시간이지만, 이를 실천하는 사람은 거의 없습니다.

title: W1. 소개와 로드맵
text:
2) 프로젝트 구성

title: 고급 생물정보학 (융합형 의사과학자 양성 사업)
text:
지난 학기에는 조직에서 카운트 데이터를 얻고 순위가 매겨진 유전자 목록을 만드는 법을 배웠습니다. 이것은 분명 중요한 역량입니다.
이번 수업은 그보다 한 단계 위를 다룹니다. 바로 오믹스 결과가 잘못되었는지 판단하는 능력입니다.






노트두 가지 깊이와 이 수업이 가르치는 것





실행의 깊이(execution depth) — doublet detector를 조정하고, LD reference panel을 구축하며, spot deconvolution을 구현하는 일입니다. 이것은 전업으로 해야 하는 일이며 생물정보학자의 역할입니다.
판단의 깊이(judgment depth) — 실제 n은 환자 3명입니까, 세포 30,000개입니까? 이 polygenic score는 내 환자와 같은 집단으로 만들었습니까? 이 UMAP이 옆 문장을 뒷받침합니까? 이 결과가 월요일의 진료를 바꿀 수 있습니까?
→ 이 수업은 두 번째 깊이를 다룹니다. 코드는 읽고 의심할 수 있도록 제시하며, 직접 유지·관리하게 하려는 것이 아닙니다.
❌ 14회의 수업을 마친 뒤 도움 없이 spatial deconvolution pipeline을 실행할 수 있다고 약속하지 않습니다.
✅ 대신 자신의 이름이 들어갈 분석을 평가하지 못하는 사람이 되지는 않게 하겠다고 약속합니다.

title: Advanced Bioinformatics (융합형 의사과학자 양성 사업)
text:
Last semester you learned to take a tissue, get counts, and produce a ranked gene list. That is a real skill.
This course is about the layer above it: being able to tell when an omics result is wrong.






NoteTwo kinds of depth, and which one this course teaches





Execution depth — tuning a doublet detector, building an LD reference panel, implementing spot deconvolution. That is a full-time job, and it belongs to your bioinformatician.
Judgment depth — is n = 3 patients or 30,000 cells the real n? Was this polygenic score built on people like my patients? Does this UMAP support the sentence next to it? Would this change what I do on Monday?
→ This course lives on the second. Code appears so that you can read it and doubt it, not so that you maintain it.
❌ It does not promise that you will run a spatial deconvolution pipeline unsupervised after fourteen sessions.
✅ It does promise that you will never again be the person in the room who cannot evaluate the analysis their own name will appear on.

title: W1. Introduction & Roadmap
section: 1) What last semester actually gave you
text:
1) What last semester actually gave you
You can take a tissue, get counts, and produce a ranked gene list. That is a real skill, and most clinicians do not have it.
It is also a single measurement of a mixture, and it answers exactly one question: which genes differ on average between these two groups of tissue?



Every remaining week of this course attacks that same gene list from a different side.


💡 Notice that none of the six questions on the right is answered by better statistics on the left. They need different data.

title: W1. Introduction & Roadmap
section: 2) The five stages have not changed
text:
2) The five stages have not changed
Whatever the technology — genotypes, chromatin, single cells, peptides — the pipeline shape is the same one you already know:
① Quality control     → is this data usable at all?
② Alignment /          → where did each measurement come from,
   quantification         and how much of it is there?
③ Normalization       → make samples comparable to each other
④ Statistical testing → which differences exceed noise?
⑤ Interpretation      → what does that mean biologically?






ImportantThe stages are not equally dangerous






Stages ① ② fail loudly — the pipeline crashes, or the numbers are absurd
Stages ③ ④ fail quietly — you get a tidy table of 847 genes, sorted by adjusted p, and nothing about its appearance tells you it is wrong

⚠️ The failure mode unique to computation: the analysis always returns an answer. A failed PCR gives you an empty gel. A failed analysis gives you a figure.

title: W1. Introduction & Roadmap
text:
3) ⚠️ Two kinds of depth
“Advanced bioinformatics” could mean two very different things. This course commits to one of them.



The left column is a full-time job. The right column is the one you are uniquely qualified for.








TipWhy the right column is yours and not the analyst’s





Your analyst can tell you the pseudobulk model converged. They cannot tell you that the “depleted” cell type is the one that never survives dissociation from inflamed tissue — because they have never held the tissue.

✅ You know what the specimen went through, what the patients were on, and what the diagnosis actually means
✅ You know whether a 2% absolute risk difference changes management
❌ Nobody can supply that for you, and no method compensates for its absence

→ The gap this course closes is not a coding gap. It is a vocabulary gap — enough to ask the right question and recognise a wrong answer.

title: W1. Introduction & Roadmap
text:
1) One clinical question, eight layers
The semester is not a tour of techniques. It is one question, pursued downward until it becomes something you could actually test.



Each layer answers something the layer above it could not.


💡 Read the right-hand column downward. Notice that the answer gets narrower and more actionable at every step — from 40 loci to one gene in one cell type at one tissue location with one candidate drug.
⚠️ Notice also the W9–W10 row: protein up, mRNA flat. Layers disagree more often than papers admit, and disagreement is usually the informative part.

NoteWhat this course deliberately does not promise

title: W1. Introduction & Roadmap
text:
1) ⚠️ The timing problem



Almost every irreversible decision happens before anyone opens R.








WarningWhat “we’ll figure out the analysis later” actually costs





Three real patterns:

① “We have n = 3 per group, is that enough?” — asked after collection. For a well-powered bulk comparison in a homogeneous system, sometimes. For single-cell across conditions, ⚠️ your n is the number of donors, not cells (W5), so the answer is usually no
② “The tissue was flash-frozen.” — then scRNA-seq is off the table and it is snRNA-seq or nothing (W5). Not a disaster, but it changes what you can claim
③ “Cases were collected at hospital A, controls at hospital B.” — see §3.3. There is no fix

→ Each of these takes 30 seconds to prevent and 18 months to regret.

title: W1. Introduction & Roadmap
text:
2) Three questions that decide everything
Ask these before a single specimen is collected.
① What is my unit of replication?
The thing you can independently repeat. Usually the patient — not the cell, not the well, not the technical replicate.

⚠️ 30,000 cells from 3 patients is n = 3
⚠️ Two aliquots of the same tumour is n = 1

② What is the comparison, exactly?
Write the sentence before collecting: “I will compare ___ to ___, and I expect ___ to differ in direction ___.”

❌ “I want to profile my patients” — not a comparison
✅ “I will compare treatment-resistant to treatment-naive, matched on age and stage” — now the design follows

③ What else differs between my groups?
Everything that tracks with your grouping is a rival explanation: collection site, storage duration, sequencing run, extraction day, operator, time of day, medication.

title: W1. Introduction & Roadmap
text:
3) ⚠️ Confounding by batch



Both layouts cost the same. Only one of them can be analysed.








ImportantWhy “we’ll just correct for batch” does not save you





Batch correction estimates the batch effect from samples that share a batch but differ in group. If no batch contains both groups, there is nothing to estimate from.
The mathematics is not being difficult — the information genuinely is not in the data. ComBat, limma::removeBatchEffect, Harmony and every successor have the same limitation.
✅ The fix is free, and it is scheduling: make sure every run, every extraction day, and every site contains both groups.
💡 If a collaborator sends you data where this was violated, saying so early is a kindness. Saying so after they have written the discussion section is not.

title: W1. Introduction & Roadmap
text:
1) Reproducibility is a clinical problem
The gap between analysis and publication is typically 1–3 years. Reviewers ask for a reanalysis. A package updated. Your laptop was replaced.
Start with two habits:

Project-based working — never setwd() again
A consistent directory structure — you know where everything lives, and so does a collaborator

title: W1. Introduction & Roadmap
text:
2) R Project (.Rproj)
An .Rproj file fixes the working directory to wherever it sits.
RStudio → File → New Project → New Directory (or Existing Directory)
A structure that scales:
my_project/
├── my_project.Rproj          ← working directory anchors here
├── rawdata/                  ← never modified, never overwritten
│   └── clinical_data.xlsx
├── scripts/                  ← numbered, in run order
│   ├── 1_clean.R
│   ├── 2_analysis.R
│   └── 3_figures.R
├── analysis/                 ← intermediate .rds objects
├── results/
│   ├── figures/
│   └── tables/
└── logs/
💡 The numbering is the point. 2_analysis.R cannot be run before 1_clean.R, and six months later that ordering is the only documentation you will trust.

text:
1) No code: does your question already have an answer?

Resource
Ask it

✅ Write down, in one sentence each, what you found — and whether your planned experiment still adds something.
💡 This is not a warm-up exercise. It is the single highest-yield hour in translational research, and almost nobody spends it.

title: W2. R Scripts, AI-Assisted Coding & Reproducibility
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Write an analysis script that you (or a reviewer) can rerun in three years

Write a prompt that produces useful code instead of plausible code

title: W2. R Scripts, AI-Assisted Coding & Reproducibility
text:
1) The reviewer arrives 14 months later
Analysis code written under deadline has a predictable shape, and a predictable fate.



The right-hand file costs about ten extra minutes to write.


⚠️ Note which detail actually kills the left-hand script. Not the messy names — the undocumented exclusion. df_final[-c(3,17,22), ] is a scientific decision with no recorded reason, and it is the first thing a careful reviewer will ask about.

title: W2. R Scripts, AI-Assisted Coding & Reproducibility
text:
2) One file, one job
scripts/
├── 1_clean.R       rawdata/  →  analysis/1_clean.rds
├── 2_deseq2.R      analysis/1_clean.rds  →  analysis/2_dds.rds
├── 3_enrich.R      analysis/2_dds.rds    →  results/tables/
└── 4_figures.R     analysis/*            →  results/figures/
Every script starts with a header stating what goes in and what comes out:

# ============================================================
# 2_deseq2.R — differential expression
# Project : IBD biopsy cohort
# In      : analysis/1_clean.rds
# Out     : analysis/2_dds.rds, results/tables/de_results.tsv
# ============================================================

💡 The numbering is documentation. 3_enrich.R cannot run before 2_deseq2.R, and in eighteen months that ordering is the only description of the pipeline you will trust.

title: W2. R Scripts, AI-Assisted Coding & Reproducibility
text:
3) Named sections
Four trailing dashes turn a comment into a navigable section (⌘/Ctrl + Shift + R inserts one):

# Libraries ----
library(DESeq2)

# Load ----
dds <- readRDS(here("analysis", "1_clean.rds"))

# Filter — 3 samples excluded, RIN < 6 ----
dds <- dds[, dds$RIN >= 6]

# Test ----
dds <- DESeq(dds)

✅ Sections appear in RStudio’s outline pane. ✅ And note the third one: the reason lives in the section title, where it cannot be separated from the code.

title: W2. R Scripts, AI-Assisted Coding & Reproducibility
text:
4) Functions — when to bother
The rule is not “always write functions.” It is: the third time you copy-paste, stop.

# The pattern that goes wrong — copy-paste per cell type
cd8 <- FindMarkers(seurat, ident.1 = "CD8 T", min.pct = 0.25)
cd4 <- FindMarkers(seurat, ident.1 = "CD4 T", min.pct = 0.25)
nk  <- FindMarkers(seurat, ident.1 = "NK",    min.pct = 0.5)   # ⚠️ typo, or intentional?

# Write it once
get_markers <- function(obj, cell_type, min_pct = 0.25) {
  FindMarkers(obj, ident.1 = cell_type, min.pct = min_pct) |>
    as_tibble(rownames = "gene") |>
    mutate(cell_type = cell_type)
}

all_markers <- map_dfr(c("CD8 T", "CD4 T", "NK"), \(x) get_markers(seurat, x))

⚠️ The point is not elegance. In the copy-pasted version, min.pct = 0.5 on the third line is invisible — and it silently changes what “NK markers” means.

title: W2. R Scripts, AI-Assisted Coding & Reproducibility
text:
1) What actually changed
Vibe coding — describing what you want in natural language and iterating on what comes back — became a mainstream working style in 2025. For clinicians it removes a real barrier: syntax was never the interesting part of your question.







It genuinely removed
It did not remove




Remembering dplyr syntax
Knowing whether the analysis is appropriate


Boilerplate plotting code
Knowing what the numbers should look like


Reading error messages
⚠️ Noticing when there is no error message


Translating between R and Python
Responsibility for what you publish

title: W2. R Scripts, AI-Assisted Coding & Reproducibility
text:
2) A prompt that works
Three components: context, task, constraints.
Context: A Seurat object `seurat` with cell types in `cell_type`
         and disease status in `condition` (levels: "IBD", "control").
         Sample identity is in `sample_id`, 12 donors total.

Task:    Write a pseudobulk differential expression function that
         takes a cell type name, aggregates counts per donor,
         and returns a DESeq2 results tibble with gene symbols.

Constraints: dplyr + DESeq2 + here. Return a tibble sorted by padj.
             Comment any step where a design choice is being made.
❌ Compare: "write code for my analysis" — you will get code that runs and answers a different question.
💡 That last constraint line is worth adding every time. Forcing the model to mark its own design choices makes them visible to you.

title: W2. R Scripts, AI-Assisted Coding & Reproducibility
text:
3) ⚠️ The gate



Everything in this course depends on step ③ actually happening.








ImportantWhy “it ran” is worthless as evidence





Traditional coding errors are loud — the script stops. That trained a whole generation to treat “no error” as “correct.”
Generated code inverts this. It is fluent, idiomatic, and usually syntactically perfect. When it is wrong, it is wrong semantically: it does a coherent thing that is not the thing you asked for.

❌ A crash is a gift. It tells you exactly where to look
⚠️ A plausible data frame of the right dimensions is the dangerous outcome

→ Your verification cannot be “did it run.” It has to be “is the output the shape and magnitude I expected?” — which requires you to have formed an expectation first.

title: W2. R Scripts, AI-Assisted Coding & Reproducibility
text:
4) ⚠️ Three silent failures



All three of these run cleanly, return the right class of object, and are wrong.

title: W2. R Scripts, AI-Assisted Coding & Reproducibility
section: 5) Where it is reliable, and where it is not
text:
5) Where it is reliable, and where it is not

✅ Reliable — plotting code, data reshaping, explaining an error message, translating between languages, writing the boilerplate around a well-known package
⚠️ Check carefully — anything involving a statistical choice, a multiple-testing correction, a join key, or a package that changed API recently
❌ Do not delegate — deciding what the comparison is, deciding what n means, deciding whether the result is biologically plausible

2) Quarto, minimally
A .qmd file is prose with executable code blocks. Render it and you get HTML, PDF, or Word.
---
title: "IBD biopsy cohort — DE analysis"
format: html
---

## Results

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(tidyverse)
res <- readRDS(here::here("analysis", "2_dds.rds"))
sig <- res |> filter(padj < 0.05)
```

We identified `r nrow(sig)` differentially expressed
genes (FDR < 0.05), of which `r sum(sig$log2FoldChange > 0)` were upregulated.
quarto render report.qmd --to html
quarto render report.qmd --to docx     # for the co-author who wants Word
✅ The inline r nrow(sig) is the whole idea: the number in the sentence is computed, not typed. Change the data, re-render, and the sentence is still true.






NoteUseful chunk options





Written as a comment at the top of a chunk, prefixed with a hash and a pipe:







Option
Effect




echo: false
run the code, hide it — for a clinical audience


eval: false
show the code, don’t run it — for teaching


warning: false
suppress package chatter


fig-cap: "..."
attach a caption, so the figure travels with its meaning


cache: true
don’t re-run a slow chunk every render



💡 This course website is a Quarto project. Every page you are reading is a .qmd.

Deleting a file in a later commit does not remove it from the repository — the earlier version is still recoverable, and on a public repo, still public.

# Insert shape checks between every step, then read the numbers
cat("rows before join:", nrow(clin), "\n")

title: W2. R Scripts, AI-Assisted Coding & Reproducibility
text:
4) Before next week
W3 — GWAS & post-GWAS. No installation needed; we start in the browser.
Come with one disease you actually treat. We will look it up together in the GWAS Catalog and Open Targets.

title: W3. GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Say what a GWAS asks, and what it structurally cannot answer
Recognise a trait’s genetic architecture and why it decides the study design
⚠️ Read a QQ plot before the Manhattan plot, and say what λ is telling you
Explain why the threshold is 5×10⁻⁸ and what “suggestive” is worth
⚠️ Explain why the reported lead SNP is usually not the causal one
Follow a hit through the four post-GWAS steps to a mechanism claim
Say why a European GWAS result may not hold in your Korean patients
Look up any disease you treat in the GWAS Catalog and Open Targets in ten minutes

title: W3. GWAS & Post-GWAS
section: 1) Five things it is already doing to your practice
text:
1) Five things it is already doing to your practice

Drug target validation — targets with human genetic support are roughly twice as likely to survive to approval
Disease subtyping — the same ICD code, different genetic architecture, different biology
Risk stratification — polygenic scores in preventive medicine (🔗 W4)
Shared aetiology — genetic correlation quantifies why two of your diagnoses keep co-occurring
Causal inference — Mendelian randomization tests causality without running an RCT

💡 Open any recent Nature Medicine issue. There is a good chance GWAS data sits underneath the clinical claim, three citations down.

title: W3. GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
2) What a GWAS actually asks

“Which genetic variants are more common in people with disease X than in matched people without it?”


Compares allele frequencies at millions of variants simultaneously
Hypothesis-free — it does not know or care which gene you think matters
Its output is a list of associated loci. ⚠️ Not genes. Not mechanisms


SNP (single-nucleotide polymorphism)

A base-pair position where two or more alleles occur commonly (MAF ≥ 1%). Humans carry ~10 million common SNPs; arrays measure 0.5–5 M directly and impute the rest from a reference panel.

title: W3. GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
3) Genetic architecture decides the design









Architecture
Variants involved
Example
What you need




Monogenic
one
phenylketonuria, CF (CFTR)
family study, WES/WGS


Oligogenic
a few
some lipid traits
targeted sequencing


Polygenic
many, each small
height, T2D
a large GWAS


Omnigenic
nearly all expressed genes
most complex traits
a huge GWAS + networks









ImportantSample size is destiny, and it is not a criticism





Schizophrenia GWAS found essentially nothing at n in the hundreds, and 108 loci at n in the tens of thousands. The biology did not change.

⚠️ Most “failed” early GWAS were not wrong. They were underpowered for a polygenic architecture
💡 This is why a 200-patient single-centre GWAS is not a viable project, and why consortium membership is the actual currency in this field

→ Effect size and druggability are also unrelated. The common HMGCR variant explains ~0.26% of LDL variance. Statins are among the most consequential drugs ever made.

title: W3. GWAS & Post-GWAS
section: 1) Look at the QQ plot first
text:
1) Look at the QQ plot first
Every GWAS paper shows a Manhattan plot. The QQ plot is where the honesty lives, and it is often in the supplement.



Read left to right: is the whole distribution shifted, or only the tail?


Genomic inflation factor λ compares the median observed test statistic to the median expected under the null.

✅ λ ≈ 1.0 with a tail lift-off — well calibrated; the lift-off is real signal
❌ λ > 1.05 with the whole line raised — uncorrected population stratification or relatedness. The hits are suspect
⚠️ λ < 0.95 — over-conservative QC; you threw away power







NoteThe exception worth knowing





At very large n, mild inflation can be genuine polygenicity — if thousands of variants truly have tiny effects, the null is not the right comparison.
✅ LD-score regression separates the two by asking whether the inflation scales with LD score (polygenicity) or is uniform (confounding). A modern paper reports the LDSC intercept alongside λ. Its absence is a fair question at review.

title: W3. GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
2) Then the Manhattan plot



Each point is a variant; height is −log₁₀(p), not effect size.


Why 5×10⁻⁸: after LD pruning there are roughly one million independent common-variant tests. Bonferroni gives 0.05 / 10⁶ = 5×10⁻⁸.

⚠️ That threshold is calibrated for common SNPs. Rare-variant and structural-variant tests need their own
⚠️ “Suggestive” (p < 1×10⁻⁵) is a convention, not a finding. Treat a suggestive-only result as a hypothesis







WarningPopulation stratification — the confounder that produces beautiful false positives





If cases and controls differ systematically in ancestry, then any ancestry-associated variant looks like a disease hit. With a Korean case group and a mixed control group, you will find “hits” for chopstick use.
✅ The fix: principal components on the genotypes, included as covariates.

RPython



# toy cohort so the model runs (illustration only)
set.seed(1)
n <- 2000
toy <- data.frame(SNP = rbinom(n, 2, 0.3), matrix(rnorm(n * 5), n, 5,
                  dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("PC", 1:5))),
                  age = rnorm(n, 55, 10), sex = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5),
                  batch = factor(sample(1:3, n, replace = TRUE)))
toy$disease <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1 + 0.3 * toy$SNP + 0.5 * toy$PC1))

glm(disease ~ SNP +
      PC1 + PC2 + PC3 + PC4 + PC5 +   # ancestry
      age + sex + batch,              # nuisance
    family = binomial, data = toy)

    sex + batch, family = binomial, data = toy)

title: W3. GWAS & Post-GWAS
section: 3) The QC that happened before the plot
text:
3) The QC that happened before the plot








QC step
Typical threshold
What it removes

> 95–98%

title: W3. GWAS & Post-GWAS
section: 1) What linkage disequilibrium does to you
text:
1) What linkage disequilibrium does to you
LD both enables GWAS — one measured variant tags dozens of unmeasured ones — and ruins its interpretation, because the tag and the cause are statistically identical.



Same locus, same biology, two populations.








ImportantWhat this means when you read a paper





“We identified rs1234567 as associated with disease X” almost always means:
→ “Somewhere in a haplotype block containing rs1234567 and ~40 other variants, something is doing something.”

❌ The lead SNP is the one with the smallest p-value in this sample. Re-run in another cohort and a neighbour often wins
⚠️ A paper that discusses the biology of the lead SNP specifically, without fine-mapping, is over-reading its own data
✅ Correct phrasing is “the locus”, and modern papers use it

title: W3. GWAS & Post-GWAS
section: 2) The four steps from postcode to mechanism
text:
2) The four steps from postcode to mechanism



Each step narrows the claim. Skipping one leaves a gap that reviewers find.


① Fine-mapping. Bayesian methods (SuSiE, FINEMAP) give each variant a posterior inclusion probability and return a credible set — the smallest set containing the causal variant with, say, 95% probability.

💡 A credible set of 3 is a result. A credible set of 40 is an admission
⚠️ Requires an ancestry-matched LD reference. A European panel applied to a Korean cohort corrupts the output silently
⚠️ If PIPs are spread thinly across many variants, the honest conclusion is “this locus cannot be resolved in this sample”

② Functional annotation. Where does the variant sit?







Location
Likely mechanism




Coding (missense, nonsense)
direct protein change


Splice site
altered mRNA or isoform


Promoter / 5′UTR
transcription regulation


Enhancer
regulation of a possibly distant gene


Intergenic / intronic
⚠️ unknown — needs eQTL and chromatin data



⚠️ About 90% of GWAS hits are non-coding. This single fact is why the rest of this course exists.
③ Variant → gene. An eQTL is a variant that affects a gene’s expression. Colocalisation asks whether the GWAS and eQTL signals share the same causal variant.

RPython



library(coloc)

# toy locus: 200 variants, variant 100 drives both signals (illustration only)
set.seed(2)
maf    <- runif(200, 0.05, 0.5)
causal <- seq_len(200) == 100
gwas_p <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(rnorm(200) + 8 * causal))
eqtl_p <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(rnorm(200) + 6 * causal))

snp    <- paste0("v", 1:200)

res <- coloc.abf(
  dataset1 = list(pvalues = gwas_p, N = 150000, type = "cc", s = 0.3, MAF = maf, snp = snp),
  dataset2 = list(pvalues = eqtl_p, N = 500,    type = "quant",      MAF = maf, snp = snp)
)
res$summary["PP.H4.abf"]   # > 0.8 → they share a causal variant

PP.H0.abf PP.H1.abf PP.H2.abf PP.H3.abf PP.H4.abf 
 7.94e-14  9.21e-08  8.62e-10  1.51e-09  1.00e+00 
[1] "PP abf for shared variant: 100%"
PP.H4.abf 
0.9999999 





import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm
from scipy.special import logsumexp

# toy locus: 200 variants, variant 100 drives both signals (illustration only)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
maf    = rng.uniform(0.05, 0.5, 200)
causal = np.arange(1, 201) == 100
gwas_p = 2 * norm.sf(np.abs(rng.normal(size=200) + 8 * causal))
eqtl_p = 2 * norm.sf(np.abs(rng.normal(size=200) + 6 * causal))

# coloc.abf written out (Wakefield approximate Bayes factors, coloc's default priors)
def log_abf(p, maf, N, s=None, sd_prior=0.15):
    z2 = norm.isf(p / 2) ** 2
    V = 1 / (2 * N * maf * (1 - maf))
    if s is not None:                              # case-control: scale by s(1-s), prior sd 0.2
        V, sd_prior = V / (s * (1 - s)), 0.2
    r = sd_prior**2 / (sd_prior**2 + V)
    return 0.5 * (np.log(1 - r) + r * z2)

l1 = log_abf(gwas_p, maf, 150000, s=0.3)
l2 = log_abf(eqtl_p, maf, 500)
p1, p2, p12 = 1e-4, 1e-4, 1e-5
lH = np.array([
    0,
    np.log(p1) + logsumexp(l1),
    np.log(p2) + logsumexp(l2),
    np.log(p1) + np.log(p2) + logsumexp([logsumexp(l1) + logsumexp(l2), logsumexp(l1 + l2)], b=[1, -1]),
    np.log(p12) + logsumexp(l1 + l2),
])
pp = np.exp(lH - logsumexp(lH))
print("PP.H4.abf =", round(pp[4], 3))   # > 0.8 → they share a causal variant

PP.H4.abf = 0.999






❌ The nearest gene is wrong roughly half the time. Enhancers routinely skip over their neighbours
⚠️ Watch the direction: a risk allele can down-regulate a gene that appears up in patients. That incoherence often reflects an impaired protective response — and it decides agonist versus antagonist

④ Gene → cell type. Colocalisation names a gene, not a place. Frameworks such as sc-linker combine single-cell data with GWAS through stratified LD-score regression and recover microglia in Alzheimer’s, T cells in eczema. We come back to this in 🔗 W5.
⑤ Causality. Mendelian randomization uses variants as instruments: randomised at conception, so they mimic a lifelong RCT immune to lifestyle confounding.
Genetic variants  →  LDL level  →  CAD
   (instrument)      (exposure)   (outcome)
⚠️ The three IV assumptions — relevance, no confounding of the instrument, and exclusion restriction — and the third is broken by pleiotropy. MR-Egger and weighted median exist to probe exactly that. A single-method MR result is incomplete.

title: W3. GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
1) GWAS Catalog — what is known?
ebi.ac.uk/gwas → search your disease.

① How many associations are reported? How many studies?
② Click the largest study. What was the sample size, and the ancestry?
③ Look at the reported variants. How many are labelled with a gene, and how many are intergenic?
④ ⚠️ Is there any East Asian study for your disease? What was its n compared with the European one?

text:
2) Open Targets — is there a drug?
platform.opentargets.org → your disease → the target list.

⑤ What is the top-scoring target, and which evidence types support it? (genetic, expression, literature, animal models)
⑥ Is there an approved or trial drug against it? For which indication?
⑦ 💡 Find a target with strong genetic evidence and no drug. That is a research question with a built-in justification paragraph.

title: W3. GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
3) Interrogating any locus — the checklist
Keep this for journal club:

① Replicated in an independent cohort?
② How big is the credible set — or was fine-mapping skipped?
③ Coding, regulatory, or unknown? Is there an eQTL?
④ Which gene, and which cell type? Remember: nearest ≠ causal
⑤ Effect size and direction — direction determines the drug strategy
⑥ Which ancestry, and does it match the patients you would apply it to?

title: W3. GWAS & Post-GWAS
section: 4) If you want to touch summary statistics
text:
4) If you want to touch summary statistics
Public summary statistics have one row per variant and no individual genotypes, so they are freely shareable. Download the study you chose in §7.1 — scripts/download_public_data.R handles the column-name mess for you.

RPython



library(tidyverse); library(qqman); library(here)

gwas <- read_tsv(here("rawdata", "t2d_gwas_summary.tsv"))

clean <- gwas |> filter(!is.na(P), P > 0, P <= 1, FREQ > 0.01, FREQ < 0.99)

# λ first, always
lambda <- function(p) {
  chisq <- qchisq(p, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
  median(chisq) / qchisq(0.5, df = 1)
}
cat("lambda =", round(lambda(clean$P), 3), "\n")

qq(clean$P, main = paste0("QQ — λ = ", round(lambda(clean$P), 3)), col = "#185FA5")

manhattan(clean, chr = "CHR", bp = "BP", p = "P", snp = "SNP",
          col = c("#185FA5", "#9db8d1"),
          suggestiveline = -log10(1e-5), genomewideline = -log10(5e-8))

lambda = 1.302 



















import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import chi2

gwas = pd.read_csv("rawdata/t2d_gwas_summary.tsv", sep="\t")

clean = gwas.query("P > 0 and P <= 1 and FREQ > 0.01 and FREQ < 0.99")

# λ first, always
def lam(p):
    return np.median(chi2.isf(p, 1)) / chi2.ppf(0.5, 1)
print("lambda =", round(lam(clean.P), 3))

# QQ plot
n = len(clean)
expected = -np.log10((np.arange(1, n + 1) - 0.5) / n)
observed = -np.log10(np.sort(clean.P.to_numpy()))
plt.scatter(expected, observed, s=2, c="#185FA5")
plt.axline((0, 0), slope=1, c="red")
plt.title(f"QQ — λ = {lam(clean.P):.3f}")
plt.xlabel("Expected -log10(p)"); plt.ylabel("Observed -log10(p)")
plt.show()

# Manhattan plot
d = clean.sort_values(["CHR", "BP"])
offset = d.groupby("CHR").BP.max().cumsum().shift(fill_value=0)
x = d.BP + d.CHR.map(offset)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 4))
ax.scatter(x, -np.log10(d.P), s=2, c=np.where(d.CHR % 2, "#185FA5", "#9db8d1"))
ax.axhline(-np.log10(1e-5), c="blue", lw=0.8)
ax.axhline(-np.log10(5e-8), c="red", lw=0.8)
ticks = x.groupby(d.CHR).median()
ax.set_xticks(ticks, ticks.index)
ax.set_xlabel("Chromosome"); ax.set_ylabel("-log10(p)")
plt.show()

lambda = 1.302



















✅ Change three things, and watch λ move each time:

RPython



# ① Drop the MHC — one enormous, hyper-polymorphic locus on chr6
no_mhc <- clean |> filter(!(CHR == 6 & BP > 25e6 & BP < 34e6))
cat("without MHC :", round(lambda(no_mhc$P), 3), "\n")

# ② Common variants only — rarer variants are noisier and less well imputed
common <- clean |> filter(FREQ > 0.05, FREQ < 0.95)
cat("MAF > 5%    :", round(lambda(common$P), 3), "\n")

# ③ ⚠️ λ scales with sample size. Rescale to a notional n = 1000 per group
#    so it can be compared across studies at all
n_eff  <- median(clean$N, na.rm = TRUE)
cat("lambda_1000 :", round(1 + (lambda(clean$P) - 1) * 1000 / n_eff, 4), "\n")

without MHC : 1.294 
MAF > 5%    : 1.39 
lambda_1000 : 1.0007 





# ① Drop the MHC — one enormous, hyper-polymorphic locus on chr6
no_mhc = clean.query("not (CHR == 6 and BP > 25e6 and BP < 34e6)")
print("without MHC :", round(lam(no_mhc.P), 3))

# ② Common variants only — rarer variants are noisier and less well imputed
common = clean.query("FREQ > 0.05 and FREQ < 0.95")
print("MAF > 5%    :", round(lam(common.P), 3))

# ③ ⚠️ λ scales with sample size. Rescale to a notional n = 1000 per group
#    so it can be compared across studies at all
n_eff = clean.N.median()
print("lambda_1000 :", round(1 + (lam(clean.P) - 1) * 1000 / n_eff, 4))

without MHC : 1.294
MAF > 5%    : 1.39
lambda_1000 : 1.0007





💡 ③ is the one worth remembering. A large biobank GWAS can show λ = 1.15 and be perfectly well calibrated, because λ grows with n under genuine polygenicity. λ₁₀₀₀ is what makes two studies comparable — and its absence from a paper is a fair question.

title: W3. GWAS & Post-GWAS
text:
5) Before next week
W4 — Polygenic Risk Scores. Browse pgscatalog.org for one disease and note the development-cohort ancestry. We start there.

title: W4. Polygenic Risk Scores
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Say what a PRS is, and what it changes for the patient in front of you
Recognise the four method names in a methods section without needing to implement them
⚠️ Separate the base GWAS from the target cohort — and say why that distinction decides everything
Read a PRS performance claim: incremental R², ΔAUC, calibration, and the decile trick
⚠️ Say why a European-derived PRS should not be applied to a Korean patient unchanged
Judge clinical readiness with ACCE rather than with AUC
Communicate a genetic risk result in a framing a patient can act on

title: W4. Polygenic Risk Scores
section: 1) One variant is useless. A million are not
text:
1) One variant is useless. A million are not
From 🔗 W3: GWAS reports variants at p < 5×10⁻⁸, each with an odds ratio of roughly 1.02–1.15. No single one is worth acting on.
A PRS sums them — each GWAS effect size \(\hat\beta_j\) multiplied by that person’s allele dosage \(G_{ij}\):
\[\text{PRS}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{M} \hat\beta_j \, G_{ij}\]
💡 Individually they are noise; in aggregate they carry real signal. .. the omnigenic model (🔗 W3 §1.3).

title: W4. Polygenic Risk Scores
text:
2) What it actually changes
A PRS does not tell you whether someone has a disease. It shifts a pre-test probability — the same thing a family history does, arrived at differently.







It is
It is not




A risk indicator, like LDL or a Framingham score
A diagnosis


Fixed from birth, measured once
A monitoring biomarker









TipCan PRS Guide Clinical Decisions?





High CAD PRS → ↑ CAD risk → ↑ absolute benefit from statin → ↓ Number Needed to Treat
Mega et al., Lancet 2015; Natarajan et al., Circulation 2017

title: W4. Polygenic Risk Scores
section: 1) ⚠️ Two datasets (GWAS & target samples) must be independent
text:
1) ⚠️ Two datasets (GWAS & target samples) must be independent











Important⚠️Overfitting





If any of the target individuals also contributed to the base GWAS, the score has partly memorised their disease status. Performance is inflated, sometimes dramatically.
✅ A trustworthy paper states base and target explicitly, confirms independence, and evaluates in a held-out cohort.

title: W4. Polygenic Risk Scores
text:
2) common ways to estimate PRS








Method
Idea in one line
When you see it




C+T (clumping + thresholding)
Keep one variant per LD block, drop those above a p cutoff
Older papers; still a sane baseline


PRSice-2
C+T with the threshold auto-tuned, plus standard plots
Very common in clinical papers


LDpred2
Bayesian — models LD and reweights all variants, no hard cutoff
Current default for accuracy


PRS-CSx
Continuous shrinkage across multiple ancestries at once
The one that matters for non-European cohorts









NoteDoes the method choice change your reading?





Mostly no. Differences between modern methods << the differences that follow from ancestry and cohort
Two exceptions worth flagging:

⚠️ A threshold-based method (C+T, PRSice-2): check the parameters for tuning
✅ A multi-ancestry method: the honest choice when the target is not European

title: W4. Polygenic Risk Scores
section: 1) Incremental value, not the PRS alone
text:
1) Incremental value, not the PRS alone
A PRS alone reaching AUC 0.64 sounds respectable. Age and sex alone reach about that for many diseases.
The only meaningful comparison:
Model A (clinical) : age + sex + BMI + family history + labs
Model B (clinical + PRS)

           ΔAUC  =  AUC(B) − AUC(A)
  incremental R²  =  R²(B)  − R²(A)      (Nagelkerke, for binary outcomes)

❌ “PRS AUC = 0.64” — uninterpretable on its own
✅ “Adding PRS raised AUC from 0.72 to 0.74 (p = 0.003)” — now you can judge it

💡 ΔAUC of 0.01–0.03 is typical for a good PRS. In a biobank of 400,000 that is comfortably significant, and for one patient it is often negligible.

title: W4. Polygenic Risk Scores
text:
2) Calibration — the metric nobody shows
Discrimination asks: does the model rank people correctly?
Calibration asks: are the predicted probabilities right? (prob = PRS + clinical data…)
Of the people told “10% risk over 10 years”, do about 10% develop the disease?






WarningGood discrimination with terrible calibration is easy





Look at the right-hand panel above. Both lines rank patients identically. One of them tells patients a number that is twice the truth.

⚠️ A PRS calibrated in the UK Biobank is not calibrated in a Korean hospital population — different baseline incidence, age structure, and competing risks
✅ Recalibration (updating the intercept or baseline hazard) is a routine fix — but it must be done, in a population-representative cohort
⚠️ Biobank volunteers are healthier than the general population, so absolute risks derived from them run systematically low

→ If a paper reports AUC and no calibration plot, the absolute risks it quotes are not trustworthy.

title: W4. Polygenic Risk Scores
section: 3) The framing decides what the patient hears
text:
3) The framing decides what the patient hears








Framing
Example
⚠️ Caveat




Percentile
“top 5% of PRS”
Says nothing about how much risk that is


Relative risk / OR
“2.3× the population average”
2.3 × a 0.4% baseline is still 0.9%


Absolute risk ✅
“18% over 10 years”
Needs incidence data for your population

title: W4. Polygenic Risk Scores
text:
4) ⚠️ Which deciles are being compared?



Nothing here is fabricated. All three numbers describe the same ten bars.


⚠️ A headline “5-fold increased risk” is almost always top-versus-bottom decile. Against the middle, the same score gives 2.8×. Against everyone else — which is how it would actually be used — 2.4×.
💡 Also check whether risk rises smoothly across deciles or only in the extreme tail. A score that separates only the top 1% is a screening tool for very few people.

title: W4. Polygenic Risk Scores
text:
5) Whose genomes built it?
Look for the ancestry of the base GWAS before anything else. §5 is entirely about why.

title: W4. Polygenic Risk Scores
text:
1) ACCE, not AUC
The standard framework for judging a genomic test:

Analytical validity — does the pipeline compute the score accurately and reproducibly?
Clinical validity — does the score associate with disease in the target population?
Clinical utility — does using it improve outcomes?
ELSI — ethical, legal and social implications: equity, consent, insurance, communication

💡 Most published PRSs clear the first two. The bottleneck is utility and ELSI — which is why PRS is not yet routine care despite twenty years of GWAS.

title: W4. Polygenic Risk Scores
text:
2) What the trials actually show








Trial
Setting
What it found / is testing




MI-GENES
CHD
PRS-integrated risk disclosure → lower LDL at 6 months, via earlier and longer statin use


GenoVA
6 diseases (CHD, T2D, AF, breast/colorectal/prostate cancer)
Effect of PRS results on time to diagnosis


WISDOM / PERSPECTIVE
Breast cancer
PRS-guided mammography intensity


eMERGE, Our Future Health
10 conditions / 5 M participants
Implementation at scale, not efficacy









NoteRead MI-GENES carefully





The mechanism of benefit was behavioural — patients told they were high-risk took statins earlier and stayed on them.
That is a real clinical effect. But note what it implies: much of the demonstrated value of PRS so far comes from motivating adherence to treatments we already had, not from identifying a biologically distinct group.
→ Worth remembering when a paper claims PRS “reveals a new high-risk phenotype”.

title: W4. Polygenic Risk Scores
section: 3) Where PRS is already inside a clinical equation
text:
3) Where PRS is already inside a clinical equation

✅ Breast cancer — BOADICEA / CanRisk: the one widely used equation combining PRS with family history, rare variants (BRCA1/2), and clinical factors. Lifetime risk of ER-positive disease ranges roughly 2% to 31% between bottom and top centile
✅ CHD — Pooled Cohort Equations: PRS is close to orthogonal to the clinical factors, so it can be added log-additively
⚠️ Everything else: no validated absolute-risk equation. Absolute risk has to be reconstructed from population incidence, which is exactly where calibration problems enter

title: W4. Polygenic Risk Scores
text:
4) The human barriers






Warning






⚠️ Patients hear genetics as destiny. Risk is probabilistic and modifiable — MI-GENES succeeded partly by framing it that way explicitly
⚠️ Run twenty PRSs and almost everyone is top-decile for something. Alarm fatigue, and a strong argument against untargeted panels
⚠️ Most physicians have no genomics training. Deployment needs decision support in the EHR and a trained champion in the department, not a PDF report

title: W4. Polygenic Risk Scores
section: 1) PRS does not transfer across ancestries
text:
1) PRS does not transfer across ancestries



Nothing about the score changed. Only the patients did.


The reasons are structural, not fixable by collecting more of the same people:

Allele frequencies differ — a variant common in Europeans may be rare or absent
LD patterns differ — the tag SNP no longer tags the causal variant (🔗 W3 §3.1)
Effect sizes differ — gene–environment and genetic-background interactions

title: W4. Polygenic Risk Scores
text:
2) What to do instead

✅ Prefer an ancestry-matched base GWAS — Korean or East Asian
✅ Use PRS-CSx or multi-ancestry meta-analysis when a matched base is too small
✅ Recalibrate in your own population and report ancestry-specific performance
✅ Korean resources: KoGES, Korea Biobank Array (KCHIP), National Biobank of Korea; EAS: Biobank Japan, China Kadoorie

title: W4. Polygenic Risk Scores
section: 1) No code: read a real score in the PGS Catalog
text:
1) No code: read a real score in the PGS Catalog
The PGS Catalog (pgscatalog.org) is the public registry of published scores — weights, metadata, and evaluated performance.
Pick a disease relevant to your specialty, then answer:

① How many variants does the score use? (Published scores range from 6 to over a million)
② What was the ancestry of the development cohort?
③ Has it been evaluated in an East Asian sample? What happened to the effect size?
④ Is calibration reported anywhere, or only discrimination?
⑤ Are there several scores for the same disease? Do they agree on which individuals are high-risk?

title: W4. Polygenic Risk Scores
section: 2) Minimal code: turn a score into a clinical figure
text:
2) Minimal code: turn a score into a clinical figure
prs_scores.tsv : pre-computed score table (n=40k) + clinical info IID, PRS, disease, age, sex⚠️ It is simulated — individual genotypes cannot be shared

RPython



library(tidyverse)
library(here)

prs <- read_tsv(here("rawdata", "prs_scores.tsv"))

# Standardise so the score reads as SD units — always do this before reporting
prs <- prs |> mutate(PRS_z = as.numeric(scale(PRS)))




import numpy as np, pandas as pd

prs = pd.read_csv("rawdata/prs_scores.tsv", sep="\t")

# Standardise so the score reads as SD units — always do this before reporting
prs["PRS_z"] = (prs.PRS - prs.PRS.mean()) / prs.PRS.std()




Incremental value over a clinical model:

RPython



library(pROC)

m_clin <- glm(disease ~ age + sex,         data = prs, family = binomial)
m_prs  <- glm(disease ~ age + sex + PRS_z, data = prs, family = binomial)

roc_clin <- roc(prs$disease, predict(m_clin, type = "response"))
roc_prs  <- roc(prs$disease, predict(m_prs,  type = "response"))

roc.test(roc_clin, roc_prs)   # ← the number that belongs in the abstract


    DeLong's test for two correlated ROC curves

data:  roc_clin and roc_prs
Z = -8.6164, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true difference in AUC is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.04005795 -0.02521126
sample estimates:
AUC of roc1 AUC of roc2 
  0.7382277   0.7708623 





import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from scipy.stats import norm, rankdata

m_clin = smf.logit("disease ~ age + sex",         data=prs).fit(disp=0)
m_prs  = smf.logit("disease ~ age + sex + PRS_z", data=prs).fit(disp=0)

# DeLong test for two correlated AUCs — what pROC::roc.test() runs by default
def delong(y, s1, s2):
    y = np.asarray(y, bool); m, n = y.sum(), (~y).sum()
    auc, v10, v01 = [], [], []
    for s in (np.asarray(s1), np.asarray(s2)):
        r, rp, rn = rankdata(s), rankdata(s[y]), rankdata(s[~y])
        v10.append((r[y] - rp) / n)           # per case: share of controls scored lower
        v01.append(1 - (r[~y] - rn) / m)      # per control: share of cases scored higher
        auc.append(v10[-1].mean())
    c10, c01 = np.cov(v10), np.cov(v01)
    se = np.sqrt((c10[0, 0] + c10[1, 1] - 2 * c10[0, 1]) / m +
                 (c01[0, 0] + c01[1, 1] - 2 * c01[0, 1]) / n)
    z = (auc[0] - auc[1]) / se
    return pd.Series({"AUC_clin": auc[0], "AUC_prs": auc[1], "Z": z, "p": 2 * norm.sf(abs(z))})

delong(prs.disease, m_clin.predict(), m_prs.predict())   # ← the number that belongs in the abstract

AUC_clin    7.382359e-01
AUC_prs     7.708623e-01
Z          -8.614555e+00
p           7.021404e-18
dtype: float64





Risk by decile — against an honest reference:

RPython



by_decile <- prs |>
  mutate(decile = ntile(PRS_z, 10)) |>
  group_by(decile) |>
  summarise(n = n(), cases = sum(disease), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(risk = cases / n,
         OR_vs_middle = (risk / (1 - risk)) /
                        (risk[decile == 5] / (1 - risk[decile == 5])))

ggplot(by_decile, aes(decile, OR_vs_middle)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#185FA5") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  labs(x = "PRS decile", y = "OR vs middle decile",
       title = "Risk by PRS decile — referenced to the middle, not the bottom") +
  theme_minimal()











import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

prs["decile"] = pd.qcut(prs.PRS_z, 10, labels=False) + 1
by_decile = prs.groupby("decile").agg(n=("disease", "size"), cases=("disease", "sum"))
by_decile["risk"] = by_decile.cases / by_decile.n
odds = by_decile.risk / (1 - by_decile.risk)
by_decile["OR_vs_middle"] = odds / odds.loc[5]

ax = by_decile.OR_vs_middle.plot.bar(color="#185FA5", rot=0)
ax.axhline(1, ls="--", c="k")
ax.set(xlabel="PRS decile", ylabel="OR vs middle decile",
       title="Risk by PRS decile — referenced to the middle, not the bottom")
plt.show()











✅ Now change one thing: re-run with decile == 1 as the reference and compare the top bar. That difference is the one you will meet in abstracts.






TipIf you want to build one yourself





Not required for this course, but the entry points are:

bigsnpr (R) — implements C+T and LDpred2; privefl.github.io/bigsnpr
PRSice-2 — command-line, auto-tunes the threshold; choishingwan.github.io/PRSice
PRS-CSx — Python, multi-ancestry; github.com/getian107/PRScsx

⚠️ Each needs an LD reference panel matched to your target ancestry. That requirement, not the modelling, is what usually stops a clinical project.

title: W4. Polygenic Risk Scores
text:
3) Before next week
W5 — single-cell RNA-seq: technology, QC, clustering. Install in advance:

title: W5. Single-cell RNA-seq — Technology, QC, Clustering
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Say what single cell answers that bulk structurally cannot — and when bulk is still the better buy
Choose between droplet and plate-based protocols, and ⚠️ between cells and nuclei
⚠️ Explain why dissociation changes the composition you measure
Explain what a UMI is, and why the count matrix is mostly zeros
⚠️ Read a knee plot and a QC scatter, and name the population each threshold deletes
Explain how a doublet detector works — and which doublets no detector can see
⚠️ Read a UMAP responsibly — and say what its distances do and do not mean
⚠️ Say which version of the matrix — raw, normalised, scaled, batch-corrected — each step should use
⚠️ Explain why per-cell differential expression across conditions is invalid, and what pseudobulk does instead

title: W5. Single-cell RNA-seq — Technology, QC, Clustering
section: 1) three biologies in a single number
text:
1) three biologies in a single number





① A general modest response: the case everyone implicitly assumes, and the least interesting
② A rare responsive subpopulation: usually the interesting one. In bulk it is diluted by the cells doing nothing, and often falls below significance entirely
③ A change in composition: not any novel cell types. There are simply more of one cell type
⚠️ ③ deserves attention because it is common in inflamed, fibrotic or infiltrated tissue — exactly the tissue clinicians study — and it is routinely written up as if it were ①.

title: W5. Single-cell RNA-seq — Technology, QC, Clustering
section: 2) When single cell is worth it
text:
2) When single cell is worth it
Single cell is expensive –> Be specific! Bulk can be enough in many cases
✅ Single cell is right for:

Discovering or characterising populations, including rare ones
Composition — which cell types shifted in disease
Cell-type-specific effects — a gene up in one cell type and down in another, invisible in bulk
Continuous states — activation, exhaustion, differentiation, where discrete labels fail

✅ Bulk is still right for:

A well-defined comparison in a homogeneous system (cell line, sorted population)
Deep transcript-level work — isoforms, splicing, low-expression genes
Large cohorts — n = 200 patients, where 200 single-cell runs is unaffordable







TipSorting first is badly underrated





Already know which cell type you care about?
→ FACS-sort it and run deep bulk RNA-seq. Often cheaper, deeper, and statistically cleaner than a whole-tissue single-cell experiment — and you can afford far more patients, which (§5) is where your power actually comes from.
💡 “We did single cell” is not by itself a stronger design. Sometimes it is a more expensive way to be underpowered.

title: W5. Single-cell RNA-seq — Technology, QC, Clustering
text:
2) 3′ vs. 5′ (for droplet kits)
one end of each transcript, not the full length — enough to count genes, not to see isoforms.






✅ Most single-cell data is 3′, including most public atlases. 5′ is the choice when you need clonotypes: T/B cells, tumour immunology, autoimmunity, vaccine responses
⚠️ For gene counting the two are broadly similar, but not interchangeable within one comparison — 3′ and 5′ samples mixed in one study are a batch effect by design
💡 For fixed or FFPE samples there is a third route: probe-based kits (10x Flex) that hybridise probes instead of capturing the poly(A) tail
The bead drawn in §3.2 is a 5′ bead — note the TSO at its end

title: W5. Single-cell RNA-seq — Technology, QC, Clustering
text:
3) Cells vs nuclei
⚠️ Decided at collection, not at analysis
scRNA-seq needs fresh, viable tissue dissociated into intact cells














scRNA-seq
snRNA-seq




Frozen / archived tissue
❌ needs fresh
✅


Large or fragile cells (neurons, adipocytes, myofibres, cardiomyocytes)
❌ lost in dissociation
✅


Dissociation stress response
⚠️ yes — FOS, JUN, heat-shock genes induced by the protocol
✅ minimal


Cytoplasmic transcripts
✅ captured
❌ missed


Intronic reads
low
high — nuclei are rich in unspliced pre-mRNA









WarningTwo consequences worth carrying into a design meeting






⚠️ Immediate-early genes are the classic false positive. A cluster defined by FOS, JUN and EGR1 is very often a dissociation artifact, not an “activated” state. If one condition sat on the bench longer, it will look more activated
⚠️ Depletion claims need scrutiny. “Cell type X is depleted in disease” and “cell type X is harder to release from diseased tissue” produce identical data

→ ✅ Mitigations: dissociate at low temperature with cold-active protease, keep the protocol identical across conditions, and — best — use nuclei when the tissue allows it.

title: W5. Single-cell RNA-seq — Technology, QC, Clustering
text:
4) considerations for a study design
⚠️ Your unit of replication is the donor. Everything in §5 follows from this, and it should shape the budget before it shapes the analysis.
💡 Given a fixed budget: more donors, fewer cells each beats fewer donors, more cells each for almost any question that compares conditions.
