section: 1) the standard pipeline: from Droplets to a Matrix
text:
1) the standard pipeline: from Droplets to a Matrix

so many steps😟? –> the more steps, the more errors propagate …😵‍💫

title: W5. Single-cell RNA-seq — Technology, QC, Clustering
text:
2) capturing a single-cell

① two tags: Barcodes and UMIs



One gel bead per droplet (a 5′ bead; see §2.2). Every oligo on the bead carries the same cell barcode and a different UMI. (Lower: an antibody-conjugated oligo, which reads out surface protein with the same barcode, as in CITE-seq.)



Cell barcode — identical on every oligo of one bead → every molecule captured in that droplet is tagged “from this cell”
UMI (unique molecular identifier) — random, different on every oligo → tags each original mRNA molecule before amplification

✅ The matrix counts molecules, not reads — PCR duplicates and amplification bias are removed
⚠️ What UMIs cannot fix: a molecule that was never captured gets no UMI at all. Hence the zeros below






Warningsparsity: why the matrix is over 90% zeros





A droplet experiment detects roughly 1,000–5,000 genes per cell, out of ~20,000.
Zero count means:

Biological zero — the gene really is not expressed in that cell
Technical zero (dropout) — the transcript was there and was not captured. Droplet capture efficiency is ~10–30%






② cell calling

Which barcodes are cells, and which are empty droplets?


Droplets. Cells are loaded dilute on purpose
Barcode rank plot (knee plot). Rank every barcode by total UMI count and plot on log–log axes:







① High plateau — real cells
② Steep drop (the knee) — the transition
③ Long low tail — empty droplets carrying only ambient RNA

⚠️ A hard cut at the knee deletes real cells that simply have little RNA — small or quiescent cells, neutrophils. They sit exactly in the transition zone.
✅ EmptyDrops (Cell Ranger ≥ 3 uses a version of it) asks a better question: not “is the total high?” but “is this barcode’s profile different from the ambient profile?” A small cell with a distinct profile is kept even though its total is low.
💡 Cell Ranger writes two matrices: filtered_feature_bc_matrix (called cells) and raw_feature_bc_matrix (every barcode). Keep the raw one — ambient-RNA correction needs the empty droplets.


③ removal of ambient RNA
Cells that burst during dissociation and loading release their mRNA into the suspension. This “soup” is captured in every droplet, so every cell’s profile = its own RNA + a little soup.






What it looks like — markers of the most abundant or most fragile cell type at low level in every cluster: haemoglobin genes in every cell of a bloody sample, ALB in the immune cells of a liver
Why it matters — false co-expression, blurred cluster boundaries, and ⚠️ false DE when one condition releases more soup (diseased, necrotic tissue usually does)

⚠️ every droplet-based protocol has it, and snRNA-seq the most (isolating nuclei lyses every cell)
💡 Well-based platforms (BD Rhapsody, plate-based Smart-seq) usually skip this step. Cells settle or are sorted into separate wells carrying little of the surrounding buffer, so far less soup is captured than in a droplet, which seals the buffer in with the cell. ⚠️ Less is not zero — the same symptom (one cell type’s markers everywhere) still means contamination.








Tool
Input
Idea




SoupX
raw + filtered matrix, clusters
Estimates the soup from empty droplets, then subtracts a contamination fraction


CellBender
raw matrix
Generative model that calls cells and removes ambient RNA in one step; GPU recommended


DecontX
filtered matrix (raw optional)
Bayesian; usable when the empty droplets were not kept



✅ Run it before QC and clustering, on each sample separately — the corrected counts are the input to everything below.

title: W5. Single-cell RNA-seq — Technology, QC, Clustering
text:
3) data QC: your own cutoffs

① low-quality QC
Three numbers per cell:









Metric
Seurat / scanpy
Too low →
Too high →




Total UMIs
nCount_RNA / total_counts
empty droplet, debris, broken cell
doublet — or a large, active cell


Genes detected
nFeature_RNA / n_genes_by_counts
as above
as above


Mitochondrial %
percent.mt / pct_counts_mt
—
dying cell — or a mitochondria-rich one



Why a high mito fraction means a dying cell: when the membrane breaks, cytoplasmic mRNA leaks out, but transcripts inside mitochondria are protected by the mitochondrial membrane and stay. The fraction rises — not because the cell made more.
⚠️ Read them jointly. High mito and few genes = broken cell. High mito with a normal gene count may be a genuinely mitochondria-rich cell (cardiomyocyte, hepatocyte, renal tubule)
⚠️ snRNA-seq: nuclei contain no mitochondria, so mito reads should be near zero. Any real fraction is cytoplasmic or ambient contamination → a much stricter cut
✅ Data-driven cutoffs: flag cells more than k median absolute deviations (MADs) from the median (scater::isOutlier; k = 3 strict … 5 permissive) — the threshold adapts to each sample
✅ Per sample, always. A more deeply sequenced sample shifts all three distributions











ImportantEvery threshold needs its rationale






A mito cutoff of 5% is conventional — and wrong for cardiomyocytes, which are genuinely mitochondria-rich. need to set your data-specific cutoffs
min.features = 500 removes debris — and also platelets, some granulocytes, and any small low-RNA cell
An upper nFeature cutoff removes doublets — and also genuinely large, transcriptionally active cells

✅ Plot the distribution, look at what sits outside your proposed cut → decide your own thresholds





② doublets
Two cells in one droplet share a barcode and look like one cell with a hybrid profile. The rate rises with loading: ~0.8% per 1,000 cells recovered on standard 10x — 10,000 cells → ~8% doublets.









Heterotypic
Homotypic




Made of
two different cell types (T cell + monocyte)
two cells of the same type


Looks like
markers of both types; a fake “intermediate” cluster or a bridge between clusters
one cell with ~2× the counts


Detectable from expression
✅ yes
❌ almost never


Damage
⚠️ invented cell types and transitions
mild



The core idea: we never see which barcodes are doublets — but we can make doublets, and then ask which real cells look like them.



A real cell surrounded by artificial doublets in PC space is probably a doublet itself.


DoubletFinder — the logic in four steps

Simulate — make artificial doublets by averaging the profiles of random pairs of real cells (pN, default 25% of the merged data)
Embed together — real + artificial cells → normalise, HVGs, PCA
Count fake neighbours — for each real cell, pANN = the proportion of artificial doublets among its nearest neighbours. A real doublet sits among the fakes → high pANN
Threshold — rank by pANN and call the top n as doublets, where n = expected rate × cells, reduced by the homotypic fraction it cannot see (modelHomotypic())

The one parameter that matters is pK, the neighbourhood size. DoubletFinder sweeps it and keeps the value at which pANN is most bimodal — singlets low, doublets high — scored by BCmvn (mean–variance-normalised bimodality coefficient).
💡 A clearly bimodal pANN distribution is your evidence that the call works. A unimodal one means doublets are not separable at that neighbourhood size.

RPython



library(Seurat); library(SeuratData); library(DoubletFinder)

# toy input (illustration only): pbmc3k as one 10x sample, after a rough pass
seu <- UpdateSeuratObject(LoadData("pbmc3k")) |>
  NormalizeData(verbose = FALSE) |> FindVariableFeatures(verbose = FALSE) |>
  ScaleData(verbose = FALSE) |> RunPCA(verbose = FALSE) |>
  FindNeighbors(dims = 1:10, verbose = FALSE) |> FindClusters(resolution = 0.5, verbose = FALSE)
seu$sample_id <- "pbmc3k"

# one sample at a time, after permissive QC, normalisation, PCA and a rough clustering
sweep <- paramSweep(seu, PCs = 1:10, sct = FALSE)
bcmvn <- find.pK(summarizeSweep(sweep, GT = FALSE))
pK    <- as.numeric(as.character(bcmvn$pK[which.max(bcmvn$BCmetric)]))

homotypic <- modelHomotypic(seu$seurat_clusters)    # share of same-type doublets
rate      <- 0.008 * ncol(seu) / 1000               # ~0.8% per 1,000 cells (10x)
nExp      <- round(rate * ncol(seu) * (1 - homotypic))

seu <- doubletFinder(seu, PCs = 1:10, pN = 0.25, pK = pK, nExp = nExp, sct = FALSE)
# → new metadata columns pANN_* and DF.classifications_* (Singlet / Doublet)
table(seu[[grep("^DF.classifications", colnames(seu[[]]), value = TRUE)]])

scDblFinder — what is different?
Same core idea (artificial doublets, and where real cells sit among them), different machinery:









DoubletFinder
scDblFinder




Artificial doublets
random pairs
random, or between clusters — focused on the heterotypic ones that matter


Score
one statistic (pANN) at one neighbourhood size
gradient-boosted classifier on kNN features at several sizes + library size, detected genes, co-expression; retrained iteratively


Parameters
pK sweep; expected n set by hand
threshold set automatically from the expected rate and misclassification


Multiple samples
run each sample yourself
samples = argument


Speed
slow (the pK sweep)
fast



DoubletFinder was the most accurate method in the first large independent benchmark (Xi & Li 2021). scDblFinder, released later, matched or beat it on the same datasets (Germain et al. 2021) and is now a common default — it is the tool in the pipeline figure.

RPython



library(scDblFinder)
sce <- scDblFinder(as.SingleCellExperiment(seu), samples = "sample_id")
seu$doublet <- sce$scDblFinder.class                # "singlet" / "doublet"
table(seu$doublet)

WarningRules for any doublet detector





⚠️ One sample (capture) at a time. Doublets form only within a capture; artificial doublets between two patients describe cells that cannot exist
⚠️ Homotypic doublets survive every expression-based method. Accept a residual
⚠️ Do it before you interpret clusters. A doublet cluster sits between its two parents and is easily named a transitional state
💡 Design beats algorithms. Pool donors in one lane and demultiplex by genotype (demuxlet, souporcell, vireo) or by hashtag antibodies → every between-donor doublet is identified directly, and you can load more cells per lane





③ Recap








Problem
What it looks like
What to do




Empty droplets
Low-UMI barcodes below the knee
EmptyDrops, not a hard cutoff


Ambient RNA
Markers of abundant cell types appearing everywhere
SoupX, CellBender, DecontX


Doublets
High UMI and high gene count; two incompatible marker sets
scDblFinder, DoubletFinder; ~0.8% per 1,000 cells recovered


Dying cells
High mitochondrial fraction, low gene count
Threshold on mito %, tissue-specifically









TipWhich comes first — doublets or QC?





The two tools’ own documentation points in opposite directions:

DoubletFinder: remove low-quality clusters first — they distort the artificial doublets and the PCA
scDblFinder: find doublets before stringent QC — the expected rate is computed from the cells you hand it, and a doublet of one good and one bad cell is recognisable only while the bad one is still in the data

✅ The order that reconciles them — ① then ② above, as in the pipeline figure:

Primary QC, permissive — remove only obvious junk: near-empty barcodes, extreme mito
Doublet detection, per sample
Final thresholds, data-driven (MADs)
Secondary QC after clustering — drop whole clusters defined by mito or stress genes, or by two incompatible marker sets (§4.4)

💡 Either order is defensible if you state it. What is not: an upper nFeature cutoff as your only doublet filter.

title: W5. Single-cell RNA-seq — Technology, QC, Clustering
text:
4) dimension reduction
After QC: thousands of cells × ~20,000 genes, mostly zeros

① normalization & scaling









Step
What it does
Why
Seurat




Normalise
divide by the cell’s total UMIs, × 10,000, then log(1 + x)
capture efficiency differs several-fold between cells for purely technical reasons; the log tames a few huge values
NormalizeData()


Select HVGs
keep ~2,000 genes whose variance exceeds what their mean predicts
most genes are flat or noise; HVGs carry the cell-type signal
FindVariableFeatures()


Scale
per gene: subtract the mean, divide by the SD
so a highly expressed gene does not dominate PCA simply by being large
ScaleData()









Note





💡 Alternatives: SCTransform (Pearson residuals from a regularised negative binomial model — all three steps in one) and scran pooled size factors. A large benchmark found the plain shifted log + PCA does as well as or better than the sophisticated options (Ahlmann-Eltze & Huber 2023)
⚠️ ScaleData(vars.to.regress = ...) can regress out mito %, depth or cell-cycle score. Use sparingly: if the “nuisance” is correlated with biology — cycling cells in a proliferative disease — you regress out the biology too
⚠️ Three versions of the same matrix now sit side by side. §5.1 depends on knowing which is which:

counts — raw UMIs
data — log-normalised
scale.data — z-scores, HVGs only






② PCA: dimension reduction
2,000 HVGs → 10–50 principal components. Each PC is a weighted combination of genes that move together — a program, not a gene.

Denoising — single genes are noisy; correlated programs are not. Top PCs carry biology, later ones mostly noise
Speed — everything downstream (neighbours, clustering, UMAP, batch correction) runs on PCs, not genes
How many? ElbowPlot() — where the variance explained flattens. Results are fairly stable across 10–50; err high rather than low, since a rare population can live in PC 25

✅ Check what drives the top PCs. If PC1 tracks nCount_RNA or percent.mt, your main axis of variation is technical → back to QC. VizDimLoadings() shows the genes
💡 PCA is linear and its distances are meaningful — unlike UMAP (§4.3). PC space is where the analysis actually happens; UMAP is only how we look at it.


③ batch correction
With several samples, cells often group by donor or batch before cell type. Correction works on the embedding, not on the counts:

Harmony — iteratively adjusts the PCs
scVI — learns a new latent space from raw counts, with batch as a covariate
Seurat CCA / RPCA — anchors matched cells between datasets

→ for neighbours, clustering and UMAP
✅ Check first whether you need it. Colour the uncorrected UMAP by sample. If cell types already mix across samples, skip it
⚠️ Corrected values are for grouping cells, not for testing genes. DE goes back to raw counts, with donor in the model (§5.1)
⚠️ Over-correction can erase a disease-specific state → 🔗 W6 §1






NoteThe VI universe — one engine, many models





scVI is the first member of a family (the scvi-tools library). All share one engine:

A variational autoencoder (VAE) — a neural network compresses each cell’s raw counts into ~10–30 latent numbers, and a decoder reconstructs the counts with a negative binomial model
Batch is handed to the decoder as an input, so the latent space does not have to encode it — that is the integration
Change the likelihood or add a modality → a new model










Model
Data
Used for
In this course




scVI
scRNA-seq
integration, denoised expression, DE
here, W6


scANVI
scRNA-seq + some cell-type labels
label transfer, annotation
§4.4


scArches
new data + a trained reference model
mapping a query onto an atlas without retraining
§4.4


totalVI
CITE-seq (RNA + surface protein)
joint RNA–protein analysis; removes antibody background



PeakVI
scATAC-seq
chromatin accessibility: integration, differential accessibility



MultiVI
multiome (RNA + ATAC), paired or not
integrating multiome with single-modality data
W11


DestVI
spatial spots + scRNA reference
deconvolution, including continuous states within a cell type
W8


veloVI
spliced / unspliced counts
RNA velocity with uncertainty
W6


contrastiveVI
perturbed vs control cells
separating treatment-specific from shared variation



MrVI
many samples / donors
sample-level (donor) differences in large cohorts





💡 Practical: all of them want raw counts (keep the counts layer), run in Python (scvi-tools; a GPU helps), and reach R via reticulate or an exported .h5ad
⚠️ Same caution as any integration: the latent space is for grouping cells. A model told to remove “batch” also removes any biology confounded with batch (W6 §1)

title: W5. Single-cell RNA-seq — Technology, QC, Clustering
text:
1) neighbors for grouping cells

Clustering and UMAP never see genes. They see a graph of which cells are near which, built in PC space.







Neighbours — for each cell, the k cells closest to it in PC space (Euclidean distance on the top PCs)
kNN graph — cells are nodes; each cell is linked to its k neighbours. Seurat then reweights each link by how many neighbours the two cells share (SNN graph), which damps outliers
Why a graph — cell populations are rarely round blobs. A graph follows the shape of the data, including elongated, branching and continuous populations, and scales to millions of cells

⚠️ “kNN clustering” is a misnomer. kNN only builds the graph; clustering (next) cuts it into communities. Nor is it k-means, which needs the number of clusters in advance and assumes round clusters.
⚠️ k sets the scale (k.param = 20 in Seurat, n_neighbors = 15 in scanpy). Small k → fine local structure, more fragments. Large k → a smoother graph, and a population with fewer cells than k cannot be its own neighbourhood — its members are forced to link outside it.

title: W5. Single-cell RNA-seq — Technology, QC, Clustering
text:
2) clustering






① leiden vs. louvain
Concept only — recognise the names and know what they optimise; no need to implement them.

Both are community detection: cut the graph into groups whose cells are more densely linked to each other than chance would predict (maximising modularity)
Louvain (2008) — greedily move each cell into the neighbouring community that most improves modularity; collapse each community into one node; repeat
⚠️ Known flaw: it can return badly connected or even disconnected communities — a “cluster” whose pieces are not linked in the graph
Leiden (2019) — adds a refinement step that guarantees every community is internally connected; also faster
Defaults: scanpy → Leiden. Seurat FindClusters() → Louvain (algorithm = 1); Leiden is algorithm = 4

💡 For the biology, the choice rarely changes the conclusion. Resolution does — report both.


② resolution






key parameter for clustering: resolution

Resolution is a term inside the modularity score: higher values reward smaller communities → more clusters.
⚠️ the best resolution is up to you…

Check clusters against marker genes and known biology, not against a score
Check stability: does the cluster survive a different resolution, a different seed, a subsampled dataset?
Ask whether a “new” cluster at higher resolution has genuinely distinct markers, or just gradations of the same ones







NoteA cluster is not a cell type





Clusters can equally reflect:

cell state (activated vs resting)
cell-cycle phase
stress response (§2.3)
ambient contamination
donor identity

⚠️ Naming a cluster after its top marker gene and treating it as a cell type is how the literature accumulates cell types that do not exist.

title: W5. Single-cell RNA-seq — Technology, QC, Clustering
text:
3) UMAP

a non-linear projection of tens of dimensions into two. It preserves local neighbourhoods reasonably and global structure badly.






Why UMAP became the default for complex tissue:

It lays out the same kNN graph as clustering (§4.1) — so its islands usually agree with your clusters
Strong pull between neighbours → compact islands with clear gaps, where t-SNE spreads groups evenly over a round cloud
It starts from the graph’s own (spectral) layout, not random positions → related populations tend to land near each other, and reruns look alike
Fast — millions of cells, where t-SNE is slow

⚠️ The t-distribution is not what makes t-SNE look round — its heavy tail is what lets t-SNE open gaps at all. The rounder, looser look comes from a weaker pull between neighbours, and the arbitrary arrangement from the random start. Start t-SNE from PCA and strengthen the pull, and it looks UMAP-like.






NoteWhat a UMAP does not tell you





❌ Distances between clusters are not meaningful. Two clusters far apart are not necessarily more different than two that are close
❌ Cluster areas are not meaningful. Size reflects the embedding, not cell number
❌ Apparent bridges are not trajectories. A thin connection may be doublets, ambient RNA, or a parameter artifact
⚠️ The layout changes with parameters and random seed. n_neighbors and min_dist
→ A UMAP is a picture of your data, not a measurement of it. Any claim that matters should be supported by a number computed in the high-dimensional space.









Note





PCA, t-SNE, UMAP — and the newer ones









Method
Year
Preserves
Where you see it




PCA
1901
global, linear structure; distances meaningful
input to everything downstream; too crude to view clusters


t-SNE
2008
local neighbourhoods; global layout arbitrary
the standard before UMAP; slower


UMAP
2018
local neighbourhoods, some global structure; fast
the current default


PHATE
2019
continuous transitions and branches
development, differentiation


densMAP
2021
also local density — a homogeneous population stays tight, a heterogeneous one spreads out
when “how variable is this population” matters


PaCMAP
2021
a balance of local and global structure
general-purpose; less common in single-cell papers so far



💡 UMAP’s reputation for better global structure than t-SNE comes mostly from its initialisation, not the algorithm; t-SNE started from PCA does about as well (Kobak & Linderman 2021)
⚠️ Every one of them is still a 2D picture. The newer methods trade one distortion for another; none turns 2D distance into a measurement (Chari & Pachter 2023)

title: W5. Single-cell RNA-seq — Technology, QC, Clustering
text:
4) Annotation

Marker-based — check known markers per cluster.
✅ Transparent.
⚠️ Circular: you find the cell types you looked for
Reference-based — map onto an annotated atlas (Azimuth, SingleR, scANVI).
✅ Fast and consistent.
⚠️ Inherits the reference’s vocabulary and cannot name anything the reference lacks

💡 Use both. Disagreements between them are the informative part — that is where a genuinely novel or genuinely artifactual population sits.

title: W5. Single-cell RNA-seq — Technology, QC, Clustering
text:
1) values to use
By now each cell carries several versions of its expression (§3.4). Testing on the wrong one is a common and silent error.









Value
Where
✅ Use for
❌ Not for




Raw UMI counts
(or ambient-corrected)
counts layer (Seurat), .layers["counts"] (scanpy)
pseudobulk DE (§5.3), any count model
comparing cells directly (depth differs)


Log-normalised
data layer (Seurat), .X after normalize_total + log1p (scanpy)
cluster markers within one dataset (§5.2), feature plots
condition comparisons with cells as n


Scaled (z-scores)
scale.data layer (Seurat), .X after sc.pp.scale (scanpy)
PCA, heatmaps
any DE


Batch-corrected
(from Harmony / scVI)
reductions, e.g. harmony (Seurat), .obsm["X_pca_harmony"], .obsm["X_scVI"] (scanpy)
neighbours, clustering, UMAP
any DE


scVI normalised / denoised expression
get_normalized_expression() output, usually stored in .layers (scvi-tools)
visualisation; scVI’s own DE
standard tests that assume observed counts









Tip





⚠️ scanpy gotcha: normalize_total, log1p and scale overwrite .X in place. Copy the raw counts into .layers["counts"] before normalising — otherwise they are gone, and pseudobulk has nothing to sum.
Re-normalise after subsetting one cell type?

For sub-clustering — partly, yes. Re-run HVG selection, scaling and PCA on the subset: the HVGs of the whole tissue mostly separate cell types from each other, not states within one type
Log-normalisation itself — no. It is computed per cell, so subsetting does not change it
For DE — not relevant. Pseudobulk starts from raw counts, and DESeq2/edgeR normalise across pseudo-samples themselves

⚠️ Exception: SCTransform residuals depend on the data they were fitted on. With several SCT models (merged samples), run PrepSCTFindMarkers() before testing

title: W5. Single-cell RNA-seq — Technology, QC, Clustering
text:
2) per-cell tests











ImportantCells from one donor are not independent samples





A Wilcoxon test across 5,400 cells from 6 donors treats those cells as 5,400 independent observations. They are not — cells from the same person share that person’s genetics, environment, medication, batch and processing.
The consequence:

p-values inflated by many orders of magnitude
add cells → the p-value shrinks indefinitely
→ you are measuring how many cells you loaded, not how many people you studied

⚠️ Seurat’s default FindMarkers behaves this way.

✅ Appropriate for identifying cluster markers within one dataset — a descriptive task
❌ Not appropriate for comparing conditions

title: W5. Single-cell RNA-seq — Technology, QC, Clustering
text:
3) Pseudobulk

for each donor × cell type, sum the counts across cells.

You now have a small matrix of pseudo-samples — analyse it with DESeq2 or edgeR exactly as in last semester’s bulk workflow.

RPython



library(Seurat); library(DESeq2); library(tidyverse)

# toy input (illustration only): annotated pbmc3k split into 4 pretend donors
set.seed(1)
seurat <- UpdateSeuratObject(LoadData("pbmc3k"))
seurat <- seurat[, !is.na(seurat$seurat_annotations)]
seurat$cell_type <- seurat$seurat_annotations
seurat$sample_id <- paste0("donor", sample(1:4, ncol(seurat), replace = TRUE))

pb <- AggregateExpression(seurat,
                          group.by = c("cell_type", "sample_id"),
                          assays   = "RNA")$RNA

# then, per cell type, a completely ordinary DESeq2 run
dim(pb)   # genes × (cell type, donor) pseudo-samples

[1] 13714    36





import numpy as np

# toy input (illustration only): pbmc3k counts + its tutorial labels, 4 pretend donors
ad = sc.datasets.pbmc3k()
labels = sc.datasets.pbmc3k_processed().obs["louvain"]
ad = ad[labels.index].copy()
ad.obs["cell_type"] = labels
ad.obs["sample_id"] = np.random.default_rng(1).choice([f"donor{i}" for i in range(1, 5)], ad.n_obs)

pb = sc.get.aggregate(ad, by=["cell_type", "sample_id"], func="sum")

# then, per cell type, a completely ordinary DESeq2 run (pydeseq2)
pb.shape   # (cell type, donor) pseudo-samples × genes

(32, 32738)






Benchmarks consistently find pseudobulk controls false positives far better than per-cell tests
Mixed models with a donor random effect are a reasonable alternative — more power retained, more computation

title: W5. Single-cell RNA-seq — Technology, QC, Clustering
text:
4) Differential abundance is compositional
Often the interesting result is not that a cell type changed its expression, but that there is more or less of it.
⚠️ Proportions are compositional — one cell type expands and every other proportion falls by arithmetic alone, with no biology behind it (multivariate).

✅ Methods that handle this: scCODA, miloR, propeller, Dirichlet-multinomial models
❌ A χ² test on cell counts is not valid
⚠️ And before believing any abundance result, return to §2.3: is this composition, or is this dissociation?

title: W5. Single-cell RNA-seq — Technology, QC, Clustering
section: 1) No code: does the atlas already answer it?
text:
1) No code: does the atlas already answer it?
CELLxGENE → search a gene from your specialty.

① Which cell types express it, in which tissues?
② Is the expression broad, or confined to one population?
③ Find a dataset in your disease area. How many donors does it have — not how many cells?
④ 💡 If the atlas already answers “which cell type expresses my gene”, you have saved a grant

title: W5. Single-cell RNA-seq — Technology, QC, Clustering
text:
2) The pipeline, end to end

RPython



library(Seurat); library(SeuratData); library(tidyverse)

InstallData("pbmc3k"); data("pbmc3k")
pbmc3k <- UpdateSeuratObject(pbmc3k)   # stored in the pre-Seurat-5 format
pbmc <- pbmc3k

pbmc[["percent.mt"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(pbmc, pattern = "^MT-")

# ⚠️ LOOK before you cut
VlnPlot(pbmc, c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent.mt"), ncol = 3, pt.size = 0)

pbmc <- subset(pbmc, nFeature_RNA > 200 & nFeature_RNA < 2500 & percent.mt < 5)

pbmc <- NormalizeData(pbmc) |>
  FindVariableFeatures(nfeatures = 2000) |>
  ScaleData() |>
  RunPCA(verbose = FALSE)

ElbowPlot(pbmc, ndims = 30)

pbmc <- FindNeighbors(pbmc, dims = 1:10) |>
  FindClusters(resolution = 0.5) |>
  RunUMAP(dims = 1:10)

DimPlot(pbmc, label = TRUE)

Number of nodes: 2638
Number of edges: 95927

Running Louvain algorithm...
Maximum modularity in 10 random starts: 0.8728
Number of communities: 9

import scanpy as sc

ad = sc.datasets.pbmc3k()
sc.pp.filter_genes(ad, min_cells=3)                 # as in the Seurat object
ad.var["mt"] = ad.var_names.str.startswith("MT-")
sc.pp.calculate_qc_metrics(ad, qc_vars=["mt"], inplace=True)

# ⚠️ LOOK before you cut
sc.pl.violin(ad, ["n_genes_by_counts", "total_counts", "pct_counts_mt"], multi_panel=True)

ad = ad[(ad.obs.n_genes_by_counts > 200) & (ad.obs.n_genes_by_counts < 2500) &
        (ad.obs.pct_counts_mt < 5)].copy()

ad.layers["counts"] = ad.X.copy()
sc.pp.normalize_total(ad, target_sum=1e4); sc.pp.log1p(ad)
sc.pp.highly_variable_genes(ad, n_top_genes=2000, flavor="seurat_v3", layer="counts")
sc.pp.scale(ad, max_value=10)
sc.pp.pca(ad)

sc.pl.pca_variance_ratio(ad, n_pcs=30)

sc.pp.neighbors(ad, n_pcs=10)
sc.tl.leiden(ad, resolution=0.5, flavor="igraph", n_iterations=2)
sc.tl.umap(ad)

sc.pl.umap(ad, color="leiden", legend_loc="on data")

title: W6. Integration, Trajectory, Regulation & Communication
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Say what integration assumes, and ⚠️ recognise when it has erased the biology you were looking for
✅ Demand the two colourings that make over-correction visible
Explain what pseudotime orders — and ⚠️ why it is not time
⚠️ Say why a trajectory algorithm always returns a trajectory
Explain where RNA velocity’s direction comes from, and which of its assumptions are contested
⚠️ Separate what regulons and gene modules built from co-expression do and do not tell you
⚠️ Explain why ligand–receptor co-expression is not evidence of an interaction
Decide which of these results belongs in a grant as a hypothesis, and which belongs in a paper as a finding

title: W6. Integration, Trajectory, Regulation & Communication
text:
1) The problem integration solves
In single-cell data the donor is usually the dominant source of variation. Cells cluster by patient before they cluster by cell type — which makes the data uninterpretable as biology.
Integration methods (Harmony, scVI, Seurat RPCA, scANVI) find a shared representation in which cells of the same type from different donors sit together.

title: W6. Integration, Trajectory, Regulation & Communication
section: 2) ⚠️ Integration is an assumption in disguise
text:
2) ⚠️ Integration is an assumption in disguise



Both right-hand panels look perfectly mixed. Only one colouring reveals what happened.


The assumption: the same cell types exist in every batch, and any batch-associated variation is technical.
⚠️ That assumption fails exactly when your biology is interesting:

a disease-specific cell state
a population present only in one condition
a treatment-induced program

→ Aggressive integration merges it away, and the resulting UMAP looks beautifully mixed.






ImportantThe diagnostic, and why it is rarely shown






✅ Colour by batch and by cell type. Publish both
✅ Confirm that known cell-type markers still separate after integration
✅ Confirm that a population unique to one condition survived
✅ Benchmarks such as scIB score exactly this batch-removal / biology-preservation trade-off

⚠️ Most papers show only the batch colouring — because that is the one that demonstrates the method worked. It is also the one that cannot reveal the failure.
💡 Back to the motivating question: a perfectly mixed UMAP and a disease-specific state are in tension. Not impossible — but the paper owes you the second colouring.

title: W6. Integration, Trajectory, Regulation & Communication
section: 3) ⚠️ When integration cannot help at all
text:
3) ⚠️ When integration cannot help at all
If disease status is perfectly confounded with batch — all patients processed on one day, all controls on another — no integration method can separate them. Exactly the argument from 🔗 W1 §3.3, and just as unrecoverable here.

title: W6. Integration, Trajectory, Regulation & Communication
text:
1) The idea
Biology is dynamic; a single-cell experiment is a snapshot. If cells were caught mid-process, they can be ordered along an axis of transcriptional similarity — a pseudotime.

Stem cell → progenitor → differentiated
Naive T cell → activated → effector → exhausted
Fibroblast → myofibroblast → senescent

Tools: Monocle3, Slingshot, PAGA.

title: W6. Integration, Trajectory, Regulation & Communication
text:
2) ⚠️ The algorithm always succeeds



Same tool, same settings, same confident output.








WarningThree caveats worth stating plainly






⚠️ A trajectory algorithm returns a trajectory for any dataset, including one with no underlying process. There is no “no trajectory found” output
⚠️ Pseudotime is not time. It measures neither rate nor duration. Two cells far apart in pseudotime may be minutes or months apart in reality — or the ordering may be reversed
⚠️ The root has to be chosen by you. Reverse the root and the biology reverses with it. That choice is prior knowledge entering as if it were a result

→ ✅ Sanity check: shuffle your cell labels, or run the algorithm on a homogeneous population, and see what comes back. It is a sobering five minutes.

title: W6. Integration, Trajectory, Regulation & Communication
text:
3) RNA velocity



Where the arrows come from.


RNA velocity adds direction by comparing unspliced (new) to spliced (mature) transcripts per gene. More unspliced than steady state predicts → the gene is turning on.
⚠️ The assumptions about splicing and degradation kinetics are contested, and known to fail for some genes and systems. The arrows are also drawn on a UMAP, so they inherit every distortion from 🔗 W5 §4.3.
✅ What settles a trajectory claim: a time course, or lineage tracing. Not a better algorithm.

title: W6. Integration, Trajectory, Regulation & Communication
section: 1) Within a cell: regulons and gene modules
text:
1) Within a cell: regulons and gene modules
Co-expression inside a cell, but two different questions:









① Regulon
② Module (gene program)




Asks
Which TF switches this state on?
Which genes move together?


Direction
TF → target (directed)
none — just a group


Prior knowledge
TF list + motif database
none (unsupervised)


Typical tools
SCENIC, decoupleR
cNMF, (hd)WGCNA




① Regulons: TF-centred

Which TF is switching this cell state on?






SCENIC — three steps

Co-expression (GRNBoost2) — predict each gene’s expression from TF expression (tree-based regression) → candidate TF–target pairs. Mostly indirect correlation
Motif pruning (cisTarget) — keep only targets whose promoter region is enriched for that TF’s motif → a regulon (TF + motif-backed targets). This step is what lifts SCENIC above plain co-expression
Activity per cell (AUCell) — how strongly the regulon’s genes sit at the top of each cell’s expression ranking (AUC) → a cell × regulon matrix → cluster, colour the UMAP, compare groups

Tools: pySCENIC (Python, the one used in practice), SCENIC (R, the original, slow)






WarningReading regulons






⚠️ TF mRNA ≠ TF activity. Phosphorylation, nuclear translocation (NF-κB) and ligand binding (nuclear receptors) are invisible in RNA — and TFs are lowly expressed, so dropout is common
⚠️ A motif ≠ binding. Closed chromatin blocks it, and scRNA alone cannot tell (with multiome / scATAC: SCENIC+, beyond this course)
⚠️ Different every run. GRNBoost2 is stochastic → run it several times and keep the regulons that recur
⚠️ Circularity. Comparing regulon activity between clusters that were defined by expression → differences are guaranteed
⚠️ Comparing conditions = the W5 per-cell trap again. Aggregate per donor before testing (🔗 W5 §5.2)

💡 Lighter alternative: decoupleR + CollecTRI — no network inference; score TF activity from known TF–target sets. Fast, reproducible, runs directly on a Seurat object (§5.4). The price: answers only within known biology
✅ Validation: binding by ChIP-seq / CUT&RUN; function by TF knockout / CRISPR / Perturb-seq





② Modules: gene programs (the NMF family)

Without a TF list: find the groups of genes that move together, from the data alone






NMF (non-negative matrix factorisation)

cell × gene matrix ≈ (program usage per cell) × (gene weights per program). Every value is ≥ 0 → programs only add up and never cancel each other out → easy to read
Each cell is a mixture of programs: cell-type identity + activities (cell cycle, IFN response, hypoxia, stress…)
A cluster gives each cell one label → a state that cuts across clusters (e.g. cycling cells in two clusters) stays invisible. NMF pulls it out as its own program
cNMF (consensus NMF): run NMF many times and keep only the programs that recur — the same logic as rerunning SCENIC. It separates identity programs from activity programs
Applied: tumour meta-programs — NMF per tumour → programs that recur across a thousand tumours (cell cycle, stress, hypoxia, EMT-like, IFN…)







NoteWhy WGCNA, standard in bulk, is used less in single cells





WGCNA = gene × gene correlation network → soft threshold → modules (eigengenes) → module–trait correlation. The standard tool in bulk RNA-seq.

Sparsity — gene–gene correlations computed over individual cells are swamped by zeros and dropout → you first have to pool similar cells into metacells (hdWGCNA). Resolution goes down, and the number of choices goes up
Composition confounding — in a mixed tissue the strongest correlations come from cell-type differences → modules end up as cell-type marker sets. To be useful, it has to run within one cell type
Hard assignment — WGCNA puts each gene in exactly one module. NMF lets a gene sit in several programs and a cell mix programs → a better fit for single cells, where identity and activity overlap

💡 hdWGCNA is still the tool when you want module–condition relationships within one cell type — and the direct bridge from the WGCNA you learned for bulk









WarningReading modules






⚠️ k (the number of programs) is your choice — as arbitrary as clustering resolution. cNMF gives you a stability / error plot to choose it
⚠️ A program is not a pathway. It needs gene set enrichment to get a name — and that name is still an interpretation
⚠️ The same co-expression limit. Moving together ≠ sharing a regulator. Compare modules between conditions per donor (🔗 W5 §5.2)

title: W6. Integration, Trajectory, Regulation & Communication
text:
2) Between cells: cell–cell communication
CellPhoneDB, CellChat and NicheNet score ligand–receptor pairs between cluster pairs based on co-expression — the ligand’s mRNA is high in cluster A, its receptor’s mRNA is high in cluster B.



The arrow in the figure is doing far more work than the data supports.


💡 NicheNet is different in kind — it links the two axes: it asks whether a ligand’s (between cells) downstream target genes are induced inside the receiver cell (within a cell). Still correlative, but a stronger correlation than co-expression alone.

title: W6. Integration, Trajectory, Regulation & Communication
text:
3) Using them honestly (both)

✅ As a hypothesis generator — “which TF / which program / which axis is worth testing?” is exactly what these tools are for
✅ Validated spatially (CCC) — if the two cell types are physically adjacent (🔗 W7), the prediction becomes plausible
✅ Validated functionally — CCC: blocking antibody, receptor knockout, ligand stimulation / regulons and programs: TF knockout, Perturb-seq
❌ As a standalone result — neither “macrophages signal to T cells via TNF” nor “TF X drives the fibrosis program” is shown by co-expression

import numpy as np, pandas as pd, scanpy as sc, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import gzip, io, urllib.request
from scipy.io import mmread

# W5's pbmc3k is a single donor, so use real multi-donor PBMCs:
# Kang et al. 2018 (GEO GSE96583) — 8 donors, the unstimulated cells
geo = "https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/"
get = lambda path: io.BytesIO(gzip.decompress(urllib.request.urlopen(geo + path).read()))
X     = mmread(get("samples/GSM2560nnn/GSM2560248/suppl/GSM2560248_2.1.mtx.gz")).T.tocsr()
genes = pd.read_csv(get("series/GSE96nnn/GSE96583/suppl/GSE96583_batch2.genes.tsv.gz"), sep="\t", header=None)[1]
cells = pd.read_csv(get("samples/GSM2560nnn/GSM2560248/suppl/GSM2560248_barcodes.tsv.gz"), header=None)[0]
meta  = pd.read_csv(get("series/GSE96nnn/GSE96583/suppl/GSE96583_batch2.total.tsne.df.tsv.gz"), sep="\t")

ad = sc.AnnData(X, obs=meta.reindex(cells.values), var=pd.DataFrame(index=genes.values))
ad.var_names_make_unique()
ad = ad[ad.obs.multiplets == "singlet"].copy()
ad.obs["donor"] = ad.obs.ind.astype(str).astype("category")
ad.obs["cell_type"] = ad.obs.cell.astype("category")

sc.pp.normalize_total(ad, target_sum=1e4); sc.pp.log1p(ad)
ad.raw = ad                                        # keep all genes for later
sc.pp.highly_variable_genes(ad, n_top_genes=2000)
ad = ad[:, ad.var.highly_variable].copy()
sc.pp.scale(ad, max_value=10); sc.pp.pca(ad)

import harmonypy
z = harmonypy.run_harmony(ad.obsm["X_pca"], ad.obs, "donor").Z_corr
ad.obsm["X_pca_harmony"] = z if z.shape[0] == ad.n_obs else z.T   # harmonypy ≥ 2 already returns cells × PCs
sc.pp.neighbors(ad, use_rep="X_pca_harmony", n_pcs=20)
sc.tl.leiden(ad, resolution=0.5, flavor="igraph", n_iterations=2)
sc.tl.umap(ad)

# ✅ the two panels that must always appear together
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))
sc.pl.umap(ad, color="donor", ax=axs[0], show=False)
sc.pl.umap(ad, color="cell_type", legend_loc="on data", ax=axs[1], show=False)
plt.show()

title: W6. Integration, Trajectory, Regulation & Communication
text:
5) Before next week
W7 — spatial transcriptomics. Come with an answer to one question about your own department:

Do we have FFPE blocks with linked outcome data, and roughly how many?

Everything in W7–W8 depends on that answer.

title: W7. Spatial Transcriptomics — The Basics
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Say what spatial data restores that dissociation destroyed
Place the major platforms on the resolution-versus-breadth trade-off, and pick one for a given question
⚠️ Say why FFPE compatibility is the single most important practical fact in this chapter
⚠️ Explain why a Visium spot is not a cell, and what follows from that
⚠️ Explain how cell segmentation on single-cell platforms can create co-expression that is not there
⚠️ Recognise the physical artifacts — folds, edges, necrosis — that masquerade as biology
Say why neighbouring spots are not independent observations
Say what spatially aware clustering adds, and what its smoothing can erase
State what your n is in a spatial experiment

title: W7. Spatial Transcriptomics — The Basics
section: 1) The same cell type, two different cells
text:
1) The same cell type, two different cells



Both are annotated identically in the single-cell object.


Everything through W6 was done on cells in suspension. The protocol’s first step destroys the variable that most of your clinical intuition runs on: where the cell was.

title: W7. Spatial Transcriptomics — The Basics
text:
2) Questions only spatial can answer

Architecture — is the immune infiltrate inside the tumour, or stuck at the margin? (immune-excluded vs inflamed vs desert)
Neighbourhoods — which cell types are actually adjacent, as opposed to merely co-present
Gradients — distance from a vessel, from the invasion front, from a germinal centre
Regional heterogeneity — one part of the tumour resistant, another sensitive
Linking back to histology — the images pathologists have been reading for 150 years

💡 Notice how many of these are things a pathologist already assesses by eye. Spatial transcriptomics is, in large part, putting molecular numbers on judgements your department already makes — which is also why your pathologist is the most useful collaborator in this chapter.

title: W7. Spatial Transcriptomics — The Basics
section: 1) One trade-off, everything else is detail
text:
1) One trade-off, everything else is detail



Resolution and breadth are bought with the same budget.



Sequencing-based (Visium, Visium HD, GeoMx, Slide-seq) — capture transcripts on a grid or in chosen regions. ✅ Whole transcriptome. ⚠️ Each capture area may contain several cells
Imaging-based (Xenium, MERFISH, CosMx) — image individual molecules in place. ✅ Single-cell, sometimes subcellular. ⚠️ A targeted panel of a few hundred to a few thousand genes, chosen in advance

title: W7. Spatial Transcriptomics — The Basics
section: 2) ⚠️ FFPE is the fact that matters most to you
text:
2) ⚠️ FFPE is the fact that matters most to you
Almost every current platform works on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue.






ImportantWhy this changes what is possible in a hospital





Your pathology department is storing blocks going back years or decades, and every one of them is attached to an outcome: who responded, who relapsed, who survived.

✅ A retrospective spatial study with real outcomes is available to you now, without waiting five years to accrue a prospective cohort
✅ You can select cases by outcome — responders vs non-responders — which is a far stronger design than profiling whoever consented
⚠️ Old blocks vary in RNA quality. DV200 is the standard metric; ask for it before committing
⚠️ Ethics and consent for archived tissue is its own process. Start it early — it is usually the long pole

💡 This is the concrete answer to “what could I actually do with this?” for most residents in this course.

title: W7. Spatial Transcriptomics — The Basics
text:
3) Choosing







Your question
Platform class




“Which cell types sit where?” — markers known
✅ Imaging panel (Xenium, CosMx)


“What is transcriptionally different about this region?”
✅ Whole-transcriptome (Visium, Visium HD)


“Compare these two histologically defined regions”
✅ GeoMx — you draw the regions


“Are these two cell types touching?”
✅ Imaging; ❌ standard Visium cannot resolve it


“Screen 60 patient blocks cheaply”
⚠️ Cost dominates — talk to the core before designing

title: W7. Spatial Transcriptomics — The Basics
text:
1) The pipeline



Our Visium HD (8 µm bin) pipeline: input, tool and output at each step.



Same skeleton as scRNA-seq (🔗 W5 §3.1), with bins in place of cells — no cell calling or doublet step, because a bin is a grid square, not a captured cell
✅ Two steps the table does not show, and you should add: QC against the H&E image, and relating domains back to histology (🔗 §5)
⚠️ “Wilcoxon” for DE between domains treats every bin as independent → inflated p-values (🔗 §4.3). Pseudobulk per sample × domain is the safer row
Deconvolution, neighbourhood enrichment and cell–cell communication → 🔗 W8

⚠️ Note that standard clustering ignores coordinates entirely — it clusters spots the way Seurat clusters cells. That domains come out spatially coherent anyway is a good sign; that they do not is informative. Methods that do use the coordinates → 🔗 §4.4.

title: W7. Spatial Transcriptomics — The Basics
text:
2) Spatially variable genes
Different question from differential expression: not “does this gene differ between groups?” but “is this gene’s expression organised in space at all?”

Tools: SpatialDE, nnSVG, Moran’s I, SPARK
✅ Useful for discovery when you do not yet know which regions matter

title: W7. Spatial Transcriptomics — The Basics
text:
3) ⚠️ Neighbouring spots are not independent






ImportantSpatial autocorrelation, and why it inflates everything





Adjacent spots share diffused transcripts, share the same local tissue, and sometimes physically share cells. They are positively correlated by construction.
Any test that treats 4,000 spots as 4,000 independent observations will produce p-values as inflated as the per-cell tests in 🔗 W5 §5.2 — and for the same reason.

⚠️ “This domain has 3,412 differentially expressed genes, all p < 10⁻¹⁵” is a symptom, not a result
✅ Methods that account for spatial dependence exist (nnSVG, SPARK-X, mixed models with a spatial term)
✅ And across patients, the fix is the same one as always: aggregate to the patient, then compare patients

title: W7. Spatial Transcriptomics — The Basics
section: 4) Domains that use the coordinates, and niches
text:
4) Domains that use the coordinates, and niches



A spot’s neighbours are a second measurement of the same tissue.


The autocorrelation that inflates p-values in §4.3 is, for clustering, signal: neighbouring spots measure the same tissue again.
① Spatially aware domains — a spot’s label depends on its own expression and its neighbours’

BayesSpace — a prior that pulls neighbouring spots towards the same label
BANKSY — adds each spot’s neighbour-averaged expression as extra features, weighted by λ, then clusters as usual. λ = 0 → ordinary clustering. Runs inside Seurat (🔗 §6.5)
GraphST — a graph neural network on the spatial neighbour graph
✅ Salt-and-pepper labels become contiguous domains; noisy spots stop flipping between clusters
⚠️ The smoothness is now partly your input. A coherent domain was a good sign in §4.1 — here you asked for it
⚠️ Too much smoothing erases small structures — a tertiary lymphoid structure (TLS), a micrometastasis, a thin layer. Compare with λ = 0 before reporting a domain map

② Niches — cluster by what is around each location (the composition of the local neighbourhood) rather than by its own expression. That is where the genuinely spatial biology lives, and it needs deconvolution first. 🔗 W8.

title: W7. Spatial Transcriptomics — The Basics
section: 1) No code: look at a real section
text:
1) No code: look at a real section
10x Genomics datasets → pick any Visium or Xenium dataset with an H&E image.

① Find the H&E and the total-counts map. Do any high-count areas correspond to folds or thick regions?
② Find the clustering figure. Does any cluster trace the edge of the section?
③ How many patients contributed? How many sections each?
④ 💡 Then look at the paper’s claims and ask which of them survive ①–③

title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Explain what deconvolution estimates, and what it cannot estimate
⚠️ Say why the reference dataset determines the answer, and what to check before trusting one
Say why single-cell-resolution data is annotated rather than deconvolved, and where those labels go wrong
Distinguish a cell-type map from a niche map, and say why the second is where the biology usually is
⚠️ Test co-localisation against a null that respects tissue structure
⚠️ Say why neighbouring spots inflate significance, and what to do about it
⚠️ Compare niches between patient groups with the patient, not the spot, as the unit
⚠️ Say what a distance limit adds to ligand–receptor inference, and what it still cannot show
Place any claim on the evidence ladder from description to demonstration
Design a spatial validation step for a hypothesis generated in W5–W6

title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
text:
1) The problem, restated
From 🔗 W7 §3: a Visium spot is a mixture. Deconvolution asks what mixture of cell types best explains the observed profile — using single-cell data as the dictionary of what each cell type looks like.



The reference is not a technical detail. It is the assumption the whole result rests on.










Method
Approach
Notes




RCTD
Statistical, models platform effects
robust, widely used


cell2location
Bayesian, estimates absolute abundance
✅ gives cell numbers, not only proportions


CARD
Uses spatial correlation between spots
borrows information from neighbours


SPOTlight
NMF-based
fast


Tangram
Maps single cells onto space
useful when you have matched data



💡 Method choice matters less than reference choice. Benchmarks separate these methods by modest margins; a wrong reference changes the answer entirely.

title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
text:
2) ⚠️ Reference bias






ImportantThe failure mode with no error message





Deconvolution returns proportions that sum to one over the cell types you supplied. It has no way to report “there is something here I have never seen”.

⚠️ A cell type absent from the reference does not appear as missing. Its signal is redistributed onto whichever reference type is closest. This is the single-cell version of reference bias, one layer down
⚠️ A reference from healthy tissue applied to tumour, or from PBMCs applied to tissue-resident cells, biases every proportion at once — not just the affected type
⚠️ A reference from a different platform (Smart-seq vs 10x, cells vs nuclei) carries systematic differences into the estimates

✅ What to actually check:

Same tissue, same condition, ideally the same patients as the spatial sections
Verify with a marker gene you did not deconvolve — plot raw CD3E and see whether it lands where the T-cell proportions did
Ask whether a rare-but-important population is in the reference at all

title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
section: 3) What proportions can and cannot tell you
text:
3) What proportions can and cannot tell you

✅ “This region is enriched for macrophage signal relative to that region” — solid
✅ “Macrophage proportion correlates with distance from the invasion front” — solid, and interesting
⚠️ “This spot contains 2.3 macrophages” — only cell2location-style methods attempt absolute numbers, and with wide uncertainty
❌ “These particular macrophages express gene X” — you cannot get cell-type-specific expression out of a mixture without much stronger assumptions

title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
section: 1) The question that spatial data is actually for
text:
1) The question that spatial data is actually for
A per-spot cell-type map is useful, and it is still one location at a time. The step that uses the geometry is asking what each location is surrounded by.



The interface exists only as a mixture. No single spot defines it.


How it works: for each spot, build a vector of the cell-type composition of its neighbours (within k spots or a fixed radius), then cluster those vectors. The clusters are niches — recurrent tissue microenvironments.

Not the same as the spatially aware domains of 🔗 W7 §4.4: domains smooth the neighbours’ expression, niches cluster the neighbours’ composition

💡 Notice what the left panel hides. T cells and macrophages are present almost everywhere and dominate almost nowhere, so a “dominant cell type” map erases them entirely. The immune biology is invisible until you look at composition rather than identity.

title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
text:
2) ⚠️ Testing co-localisation honestly






WarningAgainst which null?





“Cell type A and cell type B co-occur more than expected” requires a definition of expected.

❌ Complete spatial randomness is the wrong null. Tissue is not random — it has layers, vessels, capsules, glands. Almost any two cell types will beat this null
✅ Permute labels within the tissue, preserving the overall architecture and each cell type’s total abundance
✅ Or compare against matched control tissue — the same anatomy, different disease state

⚠️ And back to the motivating question: p < 10⁻¹² across 4,000 spots is mostly telling you that you had 4,000 spots. Neighbouring spots are positively correlated by construction (🔗 W7 §4.3), so the effective sample size is far smaller than the nominal one.
→ ✅ The number that matters is the effect size, replicated across patients.

title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
text:
3) Mapping single cells into space
The reverse direction: take a cluster you found in scRNA-seq and ask where it sits.

Tangram, Seurat anchor transfer — project single-cell labels onto spatial data
✅ Genuinely useful for testing a specific hypothesis: “the exhausted CD8 state we found — is it inside the tumour or at the margin?”
⚠️ Circularity risk: if the mapping uses the same genes that defined the cluster, finding the cluster is not independent evidence

5) Before next week

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

⚠️ Say why mRNA is a limited proxy for protein, and quantify how limited
Describe what a mass spectrometer measures, in one paragraph, without hand-waving
⚠️ Explain why DDA produces missing values that look like biology
⚠️ Say why a TMT plex is a batch, and how to design around it
Say why plasma is the hardest and most clinically useful sample in proteomics
Choose between mass spectrometry and an affinity panel for a given question
⚠️ Recognise the epitope artifact that produces false pQTLs
Describe how a discovery candidate becomes a clinical assay, and what heavy-isotope standards add
Say what multiplexed tissue imaging measures, and which W7–W8 caveats it inherits
Ask a proteomics core the three questions that determine whether your study will work

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
section: 1) How well does mRNA predict protein?
text:
1) How well does mRNA predict protein?



Eight weeks of transcriptomics, and this is the strength of the link to the molecules that do the work.


Across genes within a sample, mRNA and protein abundance typically correlate at roughly r = 0.4–0.6. Correlation across samples for a single gene varies enormously — strong for some genes, effectively zero for others.






ImportantNeither result in the motivating question is wrong





They are measurements of different things.

RNA-seq measured transcription plus transcript stability
The protein assay measured the balance of translation, folding, secretion and degradation

A 3-fold mRNA increase with no protein change is a real, interpretable finding: something downstream is buffering it. That is often more interesting than agreement would have been.
⚠️ The mistake is not the discrepancy. The mistake is having written the RNA-seq result as if it were a statement about protein.

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
section: 2) Why this matters clinically, not just technically
text:
2) Why this matters clinically, not just technically

Drugs act on proteins. A target nominated purely from transcript data has skipped a step
Every biomarker you order — troponin, PSA, CRP, HbA1c — is a protein or a protein modification
Post-translational modification is invisible to RNA-seq. Phosphorylation, cleavage and glycosylation change what a protein does without changing how much of it there is
Secretion is invisible too. A cell can transcribe a cytokine and never release it (🔗 W6 §3.2)

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
text:
1) The measurement, honestly
A mass spectrometer does not read protein sequences. It weighs charged fragments extremely precisely, and software infers sequences from the weights.
protein mixture
   → digest with trypsin        (proteins are too big; peptides are not)
   → liquid chromatography      (separate peptides in time)
   → MS1: weigh the peptides    (a survey of what is eluting now)
   → MS2: fragment and weigh    (the fragment pattern identifies the sequence)
   → match against a database   → protein identities and amounts
⚠️ Three consequences of this design that matter downstream:

You measure peptides and infer proteins. Peptides shared between family members create ambiguity
Identification depends on a database. A protein form not in the database is not found
Quantification is relative unless you spike in labelled standards

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
section: 2) ⚠️ DDA and DIA — the distinction that decides your statistics
text:
2) ⚠️ DDA and DIA — the distinction that decides your statistics



The same instrument, two acquisition strategies, very different data.








WarningWhy DDA missingness is dangerous





In DDA the instrument selects the most intense precursors in each cycle. What is “most intense” depends on everything else co-eluting at that instant.

⚠️ The same sample run twice yields partly different protein lists
⚠️ Across a cohort, whether a protein was sampled correlates with total protein load, chromatography drift, and run order
⚠️ If cases and controls were run in different batches (🔗 W1 §3.3), missingness itself becomes a group difference

→ ✅ DIA fragments everything in fixed windows, so the same proteins are quantified in every run. For any clinical cohort, this is the right default — and it is the first thing to ask about someone else’s dataset.

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
text:
1) ⚠️ Affinity assays measure binding






ImportantThe epitope artifact, and why it matters in W11





An antibody or aptamer reports how much reagent bound. Usually that tracks protein abundance. Sometimes it does not.
A coding variant that alters the binding epitope reduces the signal without changing the amount of protein present. In a genetic analysis this appears as a variant that “lowers protein levels” — a false pQTL, and one that is strongly enriched for cis variants because those are the ones inside the gene.
✅ The check: for any cis-pQTL, ask whether the lead variant is a protein-altering variant in that same gene. If it is, the finding needs orthogonal confirmation — ideally by MS, which measures peptides directly.
⚠️ This matters because pQTLs are increasingly used for drug-target Mendelian randomization (🔗 W3 §3.2). An artifact here propagates into a target nomination.

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
text:
2) Cross-platform disagreement is normal
Studies comparing affinity platforms with each other, and with MS, routinely find that a substantial fraction of targets correlate poorly.

⚠️ Two papers reporting different results for the same protein may both be right about what they measured
✅ When it matters, confirm on a second platform. That is a reviewer-proof sentence in a methods section

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
section: 1) Look up a protein you order
text:
1) Look up a protein you order
Human Protein Atlas → search a biomarker you use clinically (troponin I, PSA, CA-125, NT-proBNP…).

① Which tissues and cell types express it? Is it as specific as the clinical framing implies?
② Compare the RNA and protein tissue profiles on the same page. Where do they disagree?
③ Look at the pathology section — is expression associated with survival in any cancer?

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
section: 2) Check a proteomics dataset before trusting it
text:
2) Check a proteomics dataset before trusting it
Pick any plasma proteomics paper in your field and answer:

④ Platform? MS or affinity — and if MS, DDA or DIA?
⑤ Depletion? How many proteins were quantified, and does that number make sense for the sample type?
⑥ Missing values — how many, and how were they handled? (🔗 W10 §1)
⑦ Pre-analytical — were cases and controls collected the same way, in the same place?
⑧ Batches — were groups randomised across them, or stated at all?

💡 ⑦ and ⑧ are usually either in the supplement or absent. Absence is itself an answer.

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
text:
3) Design task
Write five sentences specifying a proteomics study you could realistically run in your department: sample type, platform, n, comparison, and the one pre-analytical variable you are most worried about.
We will use these in W10.

title: W10. Clinical Proteomics & Biomarkers
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

⚠️ Explain why missing values in proteomics are not missing at random, and how the choice of imputation changes conclusions
Run a differential abundance analysis with limma and say why it is not just a t-test
⚠️ Place a biomarker claim on the discovery → verification → validation → clinical ladder
⚠️ Recognise the wrong-control-group error, and design around it
Say what an AUC of 0.94 in a discovery study is worth
Distinguish diagnostic, prognostic and predictive biomarkers — and say which one a study actually tested
Write the design for a biomarker study you could run in your own department

title: W10. Clinical Proteomics & Biomarkers
text:
1) Why they are not random
A protein is missing from a run mostly because it was below the limit of detection — that is, because it was low. Statisticians call this MNAR (missing not at random), and it is the opposite of the assumption most default methods make.

⚠️ DDA adds a second, technical layer of missingness on top (🔗 W9 §2.2) — a protein can be absent because it was not selected, not because it was low
✅ DIA data is much cleaner in this respect, which is most of why it is now the default

title: W10. Clinical Proteomics & Biomarkers
section: 2) The four choices, and what each does to your result
text:
2) The four choices, and what each does to your result






ImportantEach one is an assumption, not a cleaning step






❌ Drop any protein with a missing value. You keep only the abundant, ubiquitously detected proteins — which is exactly the opposite of the set a novel biomarker would come from
❌ Impute with the row mean. Low values get pulled up toward the middle, shrinking precisely the difference you are testing
⚠️ Impute from a low distribution (e.g. a shifted, narrowed normal, as in Perseus). Usually a reasonable match to the MNAR mechanism — and still an assumption that belongs in the methods section
✅ Model missingness explicitly — MSstats, or report a presence/absence test alongside the intensity test. Most defensible, because it stops pretending the NAs are not data

💡 The reflexive check: rerun with a different imputation and see whether your hit survives. If it does not, you have learned something important before a reviewer does.

title: W10. Clinical Proteomics & Biomarkers
section: 1) Why limma and not a t-test
text:
1) Why limma and not a t-test
Proteomics datasets are wide and short — thousands of proteins, tens of samples. A per-protein t-test is unstable because each variance estimate rests on very few observations.
limma uses empirical Bayes to shrink each protein’s variance toward the overall trend. In practice this means a protein that happens to look very consistent by chance is not automatically declared significant.

RPython



library(limma); library(tidyverse)

# toy input (illustration only): the simulated plasma panel from the hands-on below
mat  <- readRDS(here::here("rawdata", "plasma_proteomics.rds"))
meta <- readRDS(here::here("rawdata", "plasma_meta.rds"))
mat  <- mat[rowMeans(is.na(mat)) < 0.30, ]    # proteins measured in ≥ 70% of samples

# mat: log2 intensities, proteins × samples. meta: one row per sample.
design <- model.matrix(~ condition + sex + age + batch, data = meta)   # ⚠️ batch belongs here

fit <- lmFit(mat, design) |> eBayes(trend = TRUE, robust = TRUE)
res <- topTable(fit, coef = "conditioncase", number = Inf) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "protein")
res

import numpy as np, pandas as pd, pyreadr
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests

# toy input (illustration only): the simulated plasma panel from the hands-on below
mat  = pyreadr.read_r("rawdata/plasma_proteomics.rds")[None]    # proteins × samples, log2
meta = pyreadr.read_r("rawdata/plasma_meta.rds")[None]
meta["condition"] = meta.condition.cat.reorder_categories(["control", "case"])   # control = reference, as in R
mat  = mat[mat.isna().mean(axis=1) < 0.30]     # proteins measured in ≥ 70% of samples

# limma's moderated t has no maintained Python port — an ordinary linear model per protein
def fit_per_protein(mat, meta, rhs, term="condition[T.case]"):
    rows = []
    for protein, y in mat.iterrows():
        f = smf.ols(f"y ~ {rhs}", data=meta.assign(y=y.to_numpy()), missing="drop").fit()
        rows.append((protein, f.params[term], f.tvalues[term], f.pvalues[term]))
    res = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["protein", "logFC", "t", "P"]).set_index("protein")
    res["adj_P"] = multipletests(res.P, method="fdr_bh")[1]
    return res.sort_values("P")

title: W10. Clinical Proteomics & Biomarkers
text:
2) What to report

Effect size (log2 fold change) and adjusted p-value — the same discipline as DESeq2 last semester
How many proteins were tested, and how many were dropped for missingness. ⚠️ Multiple testing is over the proteins you tested, not the ones that survived (🔗 W2 §2.4)
Whether the result survives a different imputation

title: W10. Clinical Proteomics & Biomarkers
section: 1) Three kinds of biomarker, often confused
text:
1) Three kinds of biomarker, often confused








Type
Asks
Requires




Diagnostic
Does this patient have the disease now?
Cases and the right differential diagnosis, at presentation


Prognostic
What will happen to this patient?
Follow-up, outcomes, and a survival model


Predictive
Will this patient respond to this drug?
⚠️ A treated and an untreated arm — otherwise you cannot separate prediction from prognosis



⚠️ Predictive is the hardest and the most often claimed. “Responders had higher levels than non-responders” is compatible with the marker simply indicating better-prognosis disease, regardless of treatment.

title: W10. Clinical Proteomics & Biomarkers
section: 2) ⚠️ Why an AUC of 0.94 can be worthless
text:
2) ⚠️ Why an AUC of 0.94 can be worthless



The number is real. The study answered a question nobody asks.








WarningBack to the motivating question





No — not from that study.
The paper compared advanced cancer with healthy volunteers. Your patient is neither. To be useful in your clinic, the marker must separate early cancer from the conditions that mimic it, sampled at presentation.
And there is a second problem hiding underneath. If cases were bled in an oncology ward and controls at a screening centre, then collection tube, time to processing and fasting state all differ systematically between groups (🔗 W9 §5). Some of that AUC is measuring where the blood was drawn.
→ ✅ Ask: were cases and controls sampled at the same point in the care pathway, in the same place, into the same tubes?

title: W10. Clinical Proteomics & Biomarkers
section: 3) Prevalence changes everything at the bedside
text:
3) Prevalence changes everything at the bedside
AUC is prevalence-independent; positive predictive value is not.
Sensitivity 90%, specificity 90%:

  prevalence 50% (a trial cohort)   →  PPV ≈ 90%
  prevalence  1% (a screening clinic) →  PPV ≈  8%
⚠️ The same test. Ninety-two false positives per hundred positive results, and every one of them gets a CT scan.
💡 This is the calculation you can do and the bioinformatician cannot — because it needs the prevalence in your clinic.

title: W10. Clinical Proteomics & Biomarkers
text:

⚠️ The dataset is simulated (patient specimens cannot be shared), and batch is partly confounded with condition — B1 holds 28 controls and 12 cases, B2 the reverse. That is deliberate: it is what a real banked cohort looks like, because cases and controls were collected at different times.

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Distinguish sequential from joint integration, and say which your question needs
Use convergent evidence across layers to narrow a locus to a single candidate gene
⚠️ Say why an absent signal in one layer is not a negative result
Read a MOFA variance-explained plot, and ⚠️ recognise a technical factor
⚠️ Anticipate the three failures that happen before any model is fitted: n collapse, scale imbalance, uninterpretable factors
Say what integration genuinely buys, and what it cannot manufacture

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
section: 1) Sequential — each layer filters the last
text:
1) Sequential — each layer filters the last
You already did this without calling it integration. W3 narrowed a locus; W5 named a cell type; W9 asked whether the protein exists. Each layer removes candidates.

✅ Keeps your full n at every step, because each analysis uses only the samples that have that layer
✅ Every step is interpretable on its own and defensible in a methods section
✅ Layers can come from different cohorts — public eQTL data, a published atlas, your own samples
⚠️ Cannot discover a pattern that only exists across layers

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
text:
2) Joint — model the layers together
MOFA+, mixOmics/DIABLO, iCluster and similar methods find latent factors that explain variance across several layers at once.

✅ Can reveal coordinated programmes no single layer shows
✅ Unsupervised — can find structure you did not ask about (patient subtypes)
⚠️ Needs the same samples measured on every layer
⚠️ Output is a factor, not a mechanism

💡 Answer to the motivating question: usually no, not first. Sequential prioritisation answers most clinical questions, keeps your n, and produces a figure a reviewer can follow. Reach for joint modelling when you specifically suspect a cross-layer programme, or when you want unsupervised patient subtypes.

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
text:
1) Why convergence is strong evidence
Each layer has its own false positives, and they are largely independent: an eQTL colocalisation artifact has nothing to do with a proteomics artifact. A gene surviving five independent filters is unlikely to be five separate coincidences.

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
section: 2) ⚠️ Why an absence is not evidence
text:
2) ⚠️ Why an absence is not evidence






ImportantThe asymmetry that gets misread constantly





A ✕ in one column almost always means “not measured in the right context”, not “measured and absent”.

⚠️ eQTL panels come from bulk tissue — effects confined to a rare cell type are invisible
⚠️ Plasma proteomics misses low-abundance proteins entirely (🔗 W9 §3)
⚠️ Some genes have no protein product to measure
⚠️ MR needs a strong instrument; a gene without one cannot be tested, which is not the same as being tested and failing

→ ✅ Report convergence as positive evidence. Report gaps as coverage limitations, in a sentence, in the results.
⚠️ And the failure mode this creates: prioritisation pipelines systematically favour well-measured, well-studied genes. The same bias returns in W12 as network hubs.

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
text:
1) What a factor is
A latent axis along which samples vary, together with loadings saying which features in which layers drive it. The variance-explained plot says how much of each layer each factor accounts for.

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
text:
2) ⚠️ Annotate factors before interpreting them






WarningFactor 1 is almost always technical





The strongest shared source of variation in a real cohort is rarely disease. It is batch, RNA integrity, sex, or age.
✅ The annotation routine, in order:

Technical — batch, run date, RIN/DV200, operator, storage time
Demographic — age, sex, BMI, ancestry
Clinical confounders — medication, comorbidity, disease duration
Only then — disease status or outcome

⚠️ If a factor correlates with batch at r = 0.8 and with disease at r = 0.3, it is a batch factor that happens to be slightly confounded with disease. Reporting it as a “disease signature” is a real and common error.
💡 A factor that loads across several layers is more likely to be biological than one confined to a single layer — but only after steps 1–3 come back empty.

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
text:
1) Build a prioritisation table
Take one locus for a disease you treat, and fill in the table from §2 by hand, in the browser:

eQTL / locus-to-gene — Open Targets Platform (formerly Open Targets Genetics) or GTEx
Cell type — CELLxGENE
Protein — Human Protein Atlas
Direction — IEU OpenGWAS for MR results
Tractability — Open Targets target profile

✅ One row per candidate gene, one column per layer. This is an afternoon, and it is a real figure.

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
text:
3) MOFA, and annotating its factors

RPython



library(MOFA2)

# toy layers (illustration only): 60 samples × 3 omics, features × samples;
# a batch effect runs through RNA and protein, a weaker case effect through all three
set.seed(2)
n <- 60
meta <- tibble(sample = sprintf("S%02d", 1:n), batch = rep(c("B1", "B2"), each = n / 2),
               RIN = round(runif(n, 5, 9), 1), age = round(rnorm(n, 60, 10)),
               sex = sample(c("F", "M"), n, replace = TRUE), bmi = round(rnorm(n, 25, 4), 1),
               condition = sample(c("control", "case"), n, replace = TRUE))
layer <- function(p, prefix, batch_shift, case_shift) {
  m <- matrix(rnorm(p * n), p, n, dimnames = list(paste0(prefix, 1:p), meta$sample))
  b <- 1:(p / 5); k <- p / 5 + 1:(p / 10)
  m[b, ] <- m[b, ] + rep(batch_shift * (meta$batch == "B2"), each = length(b))
  m[k, ] <- m[k, ] + rep(case_shift * (meta$condition == "case"), each = length(k))
  m
}
rna_mat <- layer(500, "gene_", 2, 1); prot_mat <- layer(200, "prot_", 1.5, 1); meth_mat <- layer(300, "cpg_", 0, 0.8)

mofa <- create_mofa(list(RNA = rna_mat, Protein = prot_mat, Methyl = meth_mat)) |>
  prepare_mofa() |> run_mofa()

plot_variance_explained(mofa)          # the figure above

# ⚠️ the step that must come next
Z <- get_factors(mofa)[[1]]
covars <- meta |> select(batch, RIN, age, sex, bmi, condition)

cors <- sapply(covars, \(v) apply(Z, 2, \(f) {
  if (is.numeric(v)) abs(cor(f, v, use = "pairwise")) else summary(aov(f ~ factor(v)))[[1]][1, "F value"]
}))
round(cors, 2)     # look here before you look at biology
