from scipy.stats import f_oneway
from mofapy2.run.entry_point import entry_point

# toy layers (illustration only): 60 samples × 3 omics, samples × features;
# a batch effect runs through RNA and protein, a weaker case effect through all three
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
n = 60
meta = pd.DataFrame({"sample": [f"S{i:02d}" for i in range(1, n + 1)], "batch": np.repeat(["B1", "B2"], n // 2),
                     "RIN": rng.uniform(5, 9, n).round(1), "age": rng.normal(60, 10, n).round(),
                     "sex": rng.choice(["F", "M"], n), "bmi": rng.normal(25, 4, n).round(1),
                     "condition": rng.choice(["control", "case"], n)})
def layer(p, batch_shift, case_shift):
    m = rng.normal(size=(n, p))
    m[:, : p // 5] += batch_shift * (meta.batch == "B2").to_numpy()[:, None]
    m[:, p // 5 : p // 5 + p // 10] += case_shift * (meta.condition == "case").to_numpy()[:, None]
    return m
views = {"RNA": layer(500, 2, 1), "Protein": layer(200, 1.5, 1), "Methyl": layer(300, 0, 0.8)}

ent = entry_point()
ent.set_data_matrix([[v] for v in views.values()], views_names=list(views))
ent.set_model_options(factors=15)                  # MOFA2's default in R
ent.set_train_options(seed=1, quiet=True)
ent.build(); ent.run()

r2 = pd.DataFrame(ent.model.calculate_variance_explained()[0] * 100, index=list(views))
r2.columns = [f"Factor{k + 1}" for k in r2.columns]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2.5))
im = ax.imshow(r2, cmap="Purples", aspect="auto")
ax.set_xticks(range(r2.shape[1]), r2.columns, rotation=90); ax.set_yticks(range(len(views)), r2.index)
fig.colorbar(im, label="variance explained (%)")
plt.show()

# ⚠️ the step that must come next
Z = pd.DataFrame(ent.model.nodes["Z"].getExpectation(), columns=r2.columns)
covars = meta[["batch", "RIN", "age", "sex", "bmi", "condition"]]

cors = pd.DataFrame({name: [abs(np.corrcoef(Z[f], v)[0, 1]) if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(v)
                            else f_oneway(*(Z[f][v == g] for g in v.unique())).statistic
                            for f in Z] for name, v in covars.items()}, index=Z.columns)
cors.round(2)     # look here before you look at biology

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
text:
5) Before next week
W12 — networks and drug targets. Bring the prioritisation table from §5.1. We will ask whether the surviving gene is druggable.

title: W12. Network Analysis & Drug Targets
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Say what a biological network is built from, and ⚠️ why that construction biases every result
⚠️ Recognise the study-bias artifact behind most “hub gene” findings
Compare the three routes to drug repurposing, and say what each is worth as evidence
⚠️ Explain why direction of effect decides agonist versus antagonist
Work through six questions that separate a top-ranked gene from an actual target
Use PheWAS and loss-of-function carriers as a free safety readout

title: W12. Network Analysis & Drug Targets
section: 1) The construction, and the bias it creates
text:
1) The construction, and the bias it creates
A protein–protein interaction network is an accumulation of published experiments. STRING, BioGRID and IntAct are curated literature, plus predictions trained on that literature.
Experiments concentrate on genes people already study. So node degree tracks publication count.



The correlation is not subtle.








ImportantThe answer to the motivating question is: not at all surprised





TP53, EGFR and AKT1 come out as hubs for nearly every disease that has ever been networked. They have tens of thousands of papers each, so they have edges to everything.
⚠️ Concretely, this means:

“Hub” analyses rediscover the same genes regardless of your data
Network proximity scores favour well-studied drugs and well-studied targets
Genes with no publications have degree ≈ 0 and can never be prioritised, however important

✅ What to do:

Compare against a degree-matched null — permute while preserving each node’s degree, so “well-connected” stops being an automatic win
Prefer networks built from a single systematic experiment (a proteomics interactome, a CRISPR screen) over literature aggregates, where you can
✅ Report degree alongside any hub claim, and let the reader see it

title: W12. Network Analysis & Drug Targets
section: 2) What networks are still good for
text:
2) What networks are still good for

✅ Modules — a set of genes that interact more than expected, giving a process-level rather than gene-level result
✅ Connecting your hits — do your 40 GWAS loci converge on a pathway?
✅ Suggesting a mechanism for a gene of unknown function, from its neighbours
⚠️ Always as a hypothesis. The edges are other people’s experiments, not yours

title: W12. Network Analysis & Drug Targets
section: 1) Genetic support is the strongest route
text:
1) Genetic support is the strongest route
Targets with human genetic support are roughly twice as likely to succeed through clinical development. The mechanism is simple: a variant that alters the target is a natural, lifelong, randomised experiment in humans — the argument from 🔗 W3 §3.2.

PCSK9 — loss-of-function carriers have low LDL and low cardiovascular risk → inhibitors work
IL6R — a variant mimicking IL-6 blockade associates with lower CHD risk → tocilizumab’s cardiovascular signal

title: W12. Network Analysis & Drug Targets
text:
2) ⚠️ Direction of effect






WarningThe mistake with the worst consequences in this course





If the risk allele increases target activity, you want an inhibitor. If it decreases it, the target may be protective — and inhibiting it would make patients worse.
Two complications:

⚠️ Incoherence. A risk allele can down-regulate a gene that appears up-regulated in patients. Often that is an impaired protective response, and the therapeutic direction is the opposite of what the expression data suggests
⚠️ Tissue-specificity. Direction can differ between tissues. The relevant tissue is the one where the disease process happens (🔗 W5, 🔗 W7)

→ ✅ Establish direction from genetics plus MR, not from a fold change in patient tissue.

title: W12. Network Analysis & Drug Targets
text:
3) Signature reversal and network proximity

Signature reversal (CMap, LINCS) — find a drug whose expression signature is anti-correlated with the disease signature. ⚠️ Reference profiles come from cell lines at high doses. Useful for generating candidates; not evidence
Network proximity — is a drug’s target close to the disease module? ⚠️ Inherits every bias in §1, so it needs a degree-matched null to mean anything

title: W12. Network Analysis & Drug Targets
section: 1) No code: profile your surviving gene
text:
1) No code: profile your surviving gene
Open Targets → your gene → its target profile.

① Tractability — small molecule? antibody? Which clinical phase, for any indication?
② Safety — any flagged organ toxicity?
③ Known drugs — is something already approved against it, for anything?
④ gnomAD → LOEUF. Is the gene tolerant of loss of function?
⑤ Open Targets → the lead variant’s page → the other traits it is associated with (a PheWAS). What else does it affect?

✅ Write the answers as five sentences. That is §3’s checklist, done.

import time
from scipy.stats import spearmanr

# Is your "hub" just a well-studied gene?
# Fetch PubMed counts for the same genes and correlate with degree.
# real PubMed counts — NCBI E-utilities, as scripts/download_public_data.R does
def pubmed_count(gene):
    r = requests.get("https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi",
                     params={"db": "pubmed", "term": f"{gene}[Title/Abstract]", "retmode": "json"})
    time.sleep(0.35)                                   # 3 requests/s without an API key
    return int(r.json()["esearchresult"]["count"])

pubs = pd.Series({gene: pubmed_count(gene) for gene in deg.index})   # gene → n papers
round(float(spearmanr(np.log10(pubs + 1), deg).statistic), 3)

0.749





💡 In most literature-derived networks this correlation is strong. Report it, and your hub claim becomes credible instead of automatic.

title: W12. Network Analysis & Drug Targets
text:
3) A degree-matched null

RPython



# toy gene sets (illustration only); the rewiring null needs one connected network
g <- largest_component(g)
disease_genes <- c("TCF7L2", "PPARG", "PCSK9", "HMGCR")
drug_targets  <- c("MTOR", "EGFR", "ESR1")

observed <- mean(distances(g, v = disease_genes, to = drug_targets))

null <- replicate(1000, {
  rw <- sample_degseq(degree(g), method = "vl")   # same degrees, rewired edges
  V(rw)$name <- V(g)$name
  mean(distances(rw, v = disease_genes, to = drug_targets))
})

cat("observed:", round(observed, 2), " null mean:", round(mean(null), 2), "\n")

observed: 1.83  null mean: 1.78 





# toy gene sets (illustration only); the rewiring null needs one connected network
g = g.connected_components().giant()
disease_genes = ["TCF7L2", "PPARG", "PCSK9", "HMGCR"]
drug_targets  = ["MTOR", "EGFR", "ESR1"]

observed = np.mean(g.distances(source=disease_genes, target=drug_targets))

null = []
for _ in range(1000):
    rw = ig.Graph.Degree_Sequence(g.degree(), method="vl")   # same degrees, rewired edges
    rw.vs["name"] = g.vs["name"]
    null.append(np.mean(rw.distances(source=disease_genes, target=drug_targets)))

print("observed:", round(observed, 2), " null mean:", round(np.mean(null), 2))

observed: 1.92  null mean: 1.79





✅ If the observed proximity is not clearly better than the degree-matched null, you have measured popularity.

title: W12. Network Analysis & Drug Targets
text:
4) Before next week
W13 — interpretation and visualisation. Bring one figure from your own work or from a paper you are reading. We will take it apart.

title: W13. Interpretation & Visualisation
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

⚠️ Spot the four ways a figure routinely overstates its data
Choose a chart form from the job the data has to do
⚠️ Say why “enriched for immune response” is almost never a result
Set the right background for an enrichment test, and say why it changes the answer
Write a figure caption as one sentence — before drawing the figure
Decide what belongs in a main figure and what belongs in the supplement

title: W13. Interpretation & Visualisation
text:
1) The others, briefly

⚠️ Truncated axes. For bars, always start at zero — a bar’s length is the value. If zero is uninformative, use points or a dot plot instead
⚠️ Rainbow colour maps. Not perceptually ordered, invent boundaries where data is smooth, and fail in greyscale and for colour-vision deficiency. ✅ Use a single-hue sequential ramp for magnitude, and a two-hue diverging ramp with a neutral midpoint for signed values
⚠️ Bars that hide n. With n ≤ 10, ✅ plot the individual points. A bar plus SEM at n = 3 implies a precision you do not have

title: W13. Interpretation & Visualisation
section: 1) The background is the whole test
text:
1) The background is the whole test
Enrichment asks whether your gene list contains more of a category than expected by chance from some universe. Change the universe, change the answer.

❌ Default “all human genes” — but genes not expressed in your tissue could never have been in your list
✅ The universe is the genes you actually tested: expressed above threshold, passing filters
⚠️ In tissue-specific data this typically halves the universe, and it can remove an entire “significant” category


library(clusterProfiler); library(org.Hs.eg.db)

universe <- rownames(dds)[rowSums(counts(dds)) > 10]   # ✅ what was testable

ego <- enrichGO(gene = sig_genes, universe = universe,     # ⚠️ not the default
                OrgDb = org.Hs.eg.db, keyType = "SYMBOL",
                ont = "BP", pAdjustMethod = "BH")

ego <- simplify(ego, cutoff = 0.7)     # collapse redundant nested terms

title: W13. Interpretation & Visualisation
text:
2) GSEA on the ranked list
✅ Often better than an over-representation test: it uses the whole ranking rather than a thresholded list, so there is no arbitrary cut-off, and modest coordinated shifts are detectable.

ranks <- res |> filter(!is.na(stat)) |> arrange(desc(stat)) |>
  select(gene, stat) |> deframe()

gseaGO <- gseGO(ranks, OrgDb = org.Hs.eg.db, keyType = "SYMBOL", ont = "BP")

title: W13. Interpretation & Visualisation
text:
3) ⚠️ Then name genes
“Enriched for immune response” is compatible with almost any inflammatory tissue. “Interferon signalling, driven by IFI44L, ISG15 and MX1” is a sentence a reader can act on — and check.

title: W13. Interpretation & Visualisation
section: 1) Take apart the figure you brought
text:
1) Take apart the figure you brought
Work in pairs. For your neighbour’s figure:

① Write the caption as one sentence. Can you?
② Does the axis start at zero, and should it?
③ Can you see the n? Can you see individual patients?
④ If there is a heatmap: how were the genes chosen, and was it row-scaled?
⑤ If there is a colour scale: sequential, diverging, or rainbow — and does it match the job?
⑥ Which panel could move to the supplement without weakening the point?

title: W13. Interpretation & Visualisation

2) Rebuild one plot

library(tidyverse)

# ❌ before
ggplot(d, aes(group, value, fill = group)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "col") +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, geom = "errorbar", width = .2)

# ✅ after — the patients are visible, and n is on the axis
d |>
  mutate(group = fct_relevel(group, "control")) |>
  ggplot(aes(group, value)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .45, outlier.shape = NA, colour = "#8A7FA3") +
  geom_jitter(width = .12, size = 2.6, alpha = .85, colour = "#185FA5") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = \(x) paste0(x, "\n(n = ", table(d$group)[x], ")")) +
  labs(y = "CD8 T-cell fraction", x = NULL,
       title = "Responders have a higher CD8 T-cell fraction") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())

title: W14. Designing Your Own Project
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Narrow a broad interest into a question with a comparison, a measurement and a data source
⚠️ Judge feasibility honestly, and recognise the quadrant where most first projects die
Plan four figures before running any analysis
State which rung of the evidence ladder your project can reach, and name the next one
⚠️ Say why a negative result is a complete project
Leave with a written one-page protocol

title: W14. Designing Your Own Project
section: 1) What “data you already have” actually includes
text:
1) What “data you already have” actually includes
Residents consistently underestimate this list:

✅ The pathology archive — FFPE blocks with linked outcomes. Spatial and proteomics both work on FFPE (🔗 W7 §2.2)
✅ Residual clinical samples — banked serum or plasma, under existing consent in some institutions
✅ The EHR — labs, imaging reports, medications, outcomes, already digital
✅ Public data collected for another purpose — GEO, CELLxGENE, TCGA, the UK Biobank return files. A dataset generated to answer question A very often contains the answer to your question B
✅ Your department’s own past studies — data that was analysed once, for one aim

💡 The best resident projects usually combine one existing dataset with one clinical question nobody in the original study cared about.

title: W14. Designing Your Own Project
text:

Step

title: W14. Designing Your Own Project
text:
1) Name your rung
From 🔗 W8 §3: description → hypothesis → consistent with → supported → demonstrated.
A resident project realistically reaches ③ consistent with. That is publishable, fundable, and honest — provided you say so and name the experiment that would take it to ④ or ⑤.
⚠️ What sinks projects at review is not stopping at ③. It is writing ⑤’s verb over ③’s evidence.

title: W14. Designing Your Own Project
section: 2) ✅ A negative result is a complete project
text:
2) ✅ A negative result is a complete project






TipWhat makes a negative result complete





Not “we found nothing”. Rather:

✅ The hypothesis was specific enough to be wrong
✅ The design could have detected the effect — say how large an effect you had power for
✅ The measurement worked — positive controls behaved as expected
✅ You can say what you would do differently

→ That is a better contribution than a fishing expedition that found a p-value. And in a fourteen-week course, it is a much more achievable target.

title: W14. Designing Your Own Project
text:
1) Ten minutes each, in pairs

① State your question in one sentence. Your partner repeats it back. Did they get it right?
② Which quadrant is it in (§2)? Be honest
③ Sketch Figure 2 — the answer figure — on paper. What are the axes?
④ What is your n, and what is the unit of replication?
⑤ Name one confounder that could produce your expected result on its own
⑥ Heading 10 — what would make you stop?







WarningThe three failure modes you will hear most often today






❌ Too broad. “I want to look at the immune microenvironment.” → apply §1 until a comparison appears
❌ n is wrong. “I have 40,000 cells.” → from how many patients? (🔗 W5 §5)
❌ Data does not exist yet. “I’ll collect fresh samples.” → how many will you have in six months? Usually the honest number is under ten

title: W14. Designing Your Own Project
text:
2) Before the final session
Deliverables:

✅ One-page protocol, all ten headings
✅ Figure 1 (cohort) drafted, even roughly
✅ Figure 2 (the answer) drafted — or the caption with the number still blank
✅ A Quarto document that renders, with no hand-typed numbers (🔗 W2 §3)
✅ Code in a git repository (🔗 W2 §4) — ⚠️ with rawdata/ in .gitignore

Presentation: 15 minutes + 5 minutes questions.
Background            2 min   the clinical problem
Question              1 min   one sentence, and why it is answerable
Data & methods        3 min   what you had, what you did, what you excluded
Results             5–7 min   your four figures, one message each
Interpretation        2 min   which rung, and what would move it up
Clinical implication  1 min   what changes if this is true

title: W7. Spatial Transcriptomics — The Basics
text:
1) Spot-based platforms: a composition



The single most misread feature of spot-based spatial data.


A standard Visium spot is 55 µm across and typically contains 1–10 cells, often of several types. What you measure is their sum.






WarningThree claims that do not follow from a spot






❌ “These two genes are co-expressed” — they may be in different cells in the same spot. The single-cell co-expression fallacy (🔗 W6 §3) returns in a new costume
❌ “This spot is a macrophage” — a spot has no cell type. It has a composition
⚠️ “These cell types are interacting” — being in one 55 µm spot is weak evidence of contact. It is better than dissociated data, and it is not adjacency

→ ✅ What you can say: this region is enriched for macrophage signal. That is a real, useful, defensible claim — and getting from there to proportions is what W8 is about.

title: W7. Spatial Transcriptomics — The Basics
section: 2) ⚠️ Single-cell platforms: a cell is a drawn line
text:
2) ⚠️ Single-cell platforms: a cell is a drawn line



Imaging platforms measure molecules. The cell is drawn in afterwards.


Xenium, CosMx, MERFISH — and Visium HD — do not measure cells either. They measure molecules at coordinates (or 2 µm bins). A cell exists only after segmentation assigns each molecule to an outline.

Nucleus only (DAPI) — clean, but drops the cytoplasm → low counts
Nucleus + fixed expansion — the common default. Recovers counts, but in dense tissue the outline runs into the neighbour and takes its transcripts
Better outlines — a membrane stain, or tools that use the transcripts themselves (Baysor). Better, still not ground truth
Visium HD — 2 µm bins regrouped into cells (bin2cell, or 10x’s own segmentation) → the same problem with a different input







WarningTwo claims a segmented cell does not support on its own






❌ “Macrophages in the tumour nest express epithelial genes” — the classic spillover artefact. A thin cell squeezed between tumour cells picks up their transcripts: a doublet (🔗 W5 §3.3) in a new costume
❌ “These two cell types touch, so they are signalling” — contact is exactly where outlines are most wrong, so a ligand–receptor pair can be created by the segmentation itself

→ ✅ Before trusting cell-level results: how often does a marker that should be exclusive (e.g. PTPRC vs EPCAM) show up in the wrong cell type, and is it worse at cell–cell contacts? Then look at the outlines on the image — the same rule as the H&E in 🔗 §5.

title: W7. Spatial Transcriptomics — The Basics
text:
6) Before next week
W8 — deconvolution and integration. Bring the answer to the question from W6: how many FFPE blocks with linked outcomes does your department hold?

title: W7. 공간전사체학 — 기초
text:
1) Spot 기반 platform: 조성



Spot 기반 spatial data에서 가장 자주 잘못 읽는 부분


표준 Visium spot = 지름 55 µm, 보통 여러 type의 cell 1–10개. 측정값 = 이들의 합






경고Spot 하나로는 할 수 없는 주장 세 가지






❌ “이 두 gene이 co-expression된다” — 같은 spot 안의 다른 cell에서 나왔을 수도. Single-cell co-expression의 함정(🔗 W6 §3)이 옷만 바꿔 입고 돌아온 것
❌ “이 spot은 macrophage다” — spot에는 cell type이 없음. 조성(composition)이 있을 뿐
⚠️ “이 cell type들이 상호작용한다” — 같은 55 µm spot 안에 있다 = 접촉의 약한 근거. Dissociation data보단 낫지만 인접(adjacency)은 아님

→ ✅ 말할 수 있는 것: 이 영역에 macrophage signal이 풍부하다. 실제로 유용하고 방어 가능한 주장 — 여기서 비율까지 가는 게 W8

title: W7. 공간전사체학 — 기초
section: 2) ⚠️ Single-cell platform: cell = 그어 놓은 선
text:
2) ⚠️ Single-cell platform: cell = 그어 놓은 선



Imaging platform은 molecule을 잼. Cell은 나중에 그려 넣는 것


Xenium, CosMx, MERFISH, 그리고 Visium HD도 cell을 측정하는 건 아님. 측정값 = 좌표 위의 molecule(또는 2 µm bin). Cell은 segmentation이 molecule 하나하나를 경계선에 배정한 다음에야 생김

Nucleus만 (DAPI) — 깔끔하지만 cytoplasm을 버림 → count 낮음
Nucleus + 고정 거리 확장 — 흔한 기본값. Count는 회복되지만 빽빽한 조직에선 경계선이 이웃 cell로 넘어가 이웃의 transcript를 가져옴
더 나은 경계선 — membrane 염색, 또는 transcript 자체를 쓰는 tool(Baysor). 낫지만 여전히 정답은 아님
Visium HD — 2 µm bin을 cell 단위로 다시 묶음(bin2cell, 10x 자체 segmentation) → 입력만 다르고 같은 문제







경고Segmentation된 cell 하나로는 할 수 없는 주장 두 가지






❌ “종양 둥지 속 macrophage가 epithelial gene을 발현한다” — 대표적인 spillover artefact. 종양 cell 사이에 끼인 얇은 cell이 이웃의 transcript를 주워 담음 = 새 옷 입은 doublet(🔗 W5 §3.3)
❌ “두 cell type이 맞닿아 있으니 signalling한다” — 경계선이 가장 많이 틀리는 곳 = 바로 접촉면. Ligand–receptor 쌍이 segmentation에서 만들어질 수 있음

→ ✅ Cell 수준 결과를 믿기 전에: 배타적이어야 할 marker(예: PTPRC vs EPCAM)가 엉뚱한 cell type에서 얼마나 나오나, 접촉면에서 더 심한가? 그다음 영상 위에 경계선을 겹쳐 보기 — 🔗 §5의 H&E와 같은 원칙

title: W7. 공간전사체학 — 기초
text:
6) 다음 주 전까지
W8 — deconvolution과 integration. W6에서 던진 질문의 답 가져오기: 우리 과에 outcome이 연결된 FFPE block이 몇 개 있나?

title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
text:
4) Single-cell resolution: annotate, don’t deconvolve



On single-cell platforms the question becomes labelling, not unmixing.


On Xenium, CosMx or Visium HD the unit is a segmented cell (🔗 W7 §3.2), not a mixture. The task becomes annotation: one label per cell, from the same single-cell reference.

Label transfer (Seurat anchors, as in §2.3) or RCTD in doublet mode (each cell or 8 µm bin = one or two types) — the logic of §1.1 on a smaller unit
⚠️ Only the panel’s genes are used. The reference has ~20,000 genes, the panel a few hundred to 5,000. A cell type with no marker on the panel cannot be called — it is forced into its nearest neighbour (§1.2 again)
⚠️ The label inherits the segmentation. A cell holding its neighbour’s transcripts gets a mixed, low-confidence or wrong label
✅ Map the confidence. Low-confidence calls piling up at cell–cell contacts = segmentation spillover, not a new “hybrid” state
✅ After that, everything below — niches, co-localisation, patient comparisons — works the same, with cells in place of spots

💡 Panel design is an analysis decision made before the experiment: check that every cell type in your hypothesis has markers on the panel.

title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
text:
4) ⚠️ Comparing niches between patients



One large section from one patient can produce a tiny p on its own.


“TAM-rich niches are more common in non-responders” is a claim about patients, so the patient is the unit — the same logic as pseudobulk (🔗 W5 §5.3).

① Define niches on all sections together, so a niche label means the same thing in every patient
② Per patient: the fraction of the section in each niche → one row per patient
③ Compare groups on those rows, n = patients. Fractions are compositional (🔗 W5 §5.4) → propeller-style tests, or a model with the patient as the unit
⚠️ Pooled spots (a χ² on 5,000 spots) = W5’s per-cell test in a new costume. One big section can carry the whole result
⚠️ Several sections per patient → average them, or model the patient as a random effect. Never count them as extra patients
✅ Report the effect size with an interval, and show one dot per patient

title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
text:
5) ⚠️ Ligand–receptor, now with distance



Distance removes pairs that could never meet. It proves none of the rest.


W6’s cell–cell communication (🔗 W6 §3.2) scores every sender cluster against every receiver cluster — including cells that were never in the same place. Spatial data adds the missing constraint.

Distance limit — score only sender–receiver pairs within signalling range. Contact signals: direct neighbours. Secreted signals: further, up to a few hundred µm
COMMOT — optimal transport with a distance limit; ligands and receptors compete for each other
CellChat v2 — spatial mode, with separate ranges for contact and secreted signals
LIANA+ — local scores: where in the section are ligand and receptor high together?
✅ Test against a structure-preserving null (§2.2) — e.g. shift the receiver layer as a whole. Being near matters only if it is nearer than the tissue predicts
⚠️ Still mRNA next to mRNA: no protein, no binding, no response. A W6 hypothesis moves to rung ③ at most (🔗 §3)
⚠️ On Visium, sender and receiver can share one spot → “near” is set by 55 µm, not by biology. Single-cell platforms give the cleaner version — with the segmentation caveat of §1.4

title: W8. 디콘볼루션과 공간 통합
text:
4) Single-cell 해상도: deconvolution 말고 annotation



Single-cell platform에선 질문이 “섞인 걸 풀기”에서 “label 붙이기”로 바뀜


Xenium, CosMx, Visium HD에선 단위 = segmentation된 cell(🔗 W7 §3.2), 혼합물이 아님. 할 일 = annotation: 같은 single-cell reference로 cell마다 label 하나

Label transfer(Seurat anchor, §2.3과 같은 방식) 또는 RCTD doublet mode(cell 또는 8 µm bin 하나 = type 한두 개) — §1.1의 논리를 더 작은 단위에 적용
⚠️ Panel에 있는 gene만 쓰임. Reference는 gene ~20,000개, panel은 수백~5,000개. Panel에 marker가 없는 cell type은 부를 수 없음 → 가장 가까운 type으로 억지 배정 (§1.2 다시)
⚠️ Label은 segmentation을 물려받음. 이웃의 transcript를 담은 cell → 섞이거나, 확신 낮거나, 틀린 label
✅ Confidence를 지도에 그려보기. 확신 낮은 call이 cell–cell 접촉면에 몰려 있다 = segmentation spillover. 새로운 “hybrid” state 아님
✅ 그다음부턴 아래 내용(niche, co-localisation, 환자 간 비교)이 spot 대신 cell로 똑같이 적용됨

💡 Panel 설계 = 실험 전에 내리는 분석 결정. 가설에 나오는 cell type마다 panel에 marker가 있는지 확인

title: W8. 디콘볼루션과 공간 통합
text:
4) ⚠️ 환자 간 niche 비교



큰 절편 하나가 혼자서 아주 작은 p를 만들 수 있음


“비반응자에서 TAM-rich niche가 더 흔하다” = 환자에 대한 주장 → 단위도 환자. Pseudobulk와 같은 논리(🔗 W5 §5.3)

① Niche는 모든 절편을 합쳐서 정의 → 같은 niche label이 모든 환자에서 같은 뜻
② 환자마다 절편 중 각 niche가 차지하는 비율 → 환자당 한 줄
③ 그 줄들로 군 비교, n = 환자. 비율은 compositional(🔗 W5 §5.4) → propeller 같은 test, 또는 환자를 단위로 한 model
⚠️ Spot을 합쳐서 검정(spot 5,000개로 χ²) = W5의 per-cell test가 옷만 바꿔 입은 것. 큰 절편 하나가 결과 전체를 끌고 갈 수 있음
⚠️ 환자당 절편 여러 장 → 평균 내거나 환자를 random effect로. 절대 환자 수로 세지 않기
✅ Effect size + 구간으로 보고, 환자당 점 하나씩 보여주기

title: W8. 디콘볼루션과 공간 통합
text:
5) ⚠️ Ligand–receptor, 이번엔 거리까지



거리 = 만날 수 없던 짝을 지워줄 뿐, 나머지를 증명하진 않음


W6의 cell–cell communication(🔗 W6 §3.2) = 모든 sender cluster x 모든 receiver cluster 점수화 → 같은 장소에 있어본 적 없는 cell끼리도 포함. Spatial data가 빠진 제약을 채워줌

거리 제한 — 신호가 닿는 범위 안의 sender–receiver 쌍만 점수화. Contact 신호: 바로 옆 cell. 분비 신호: 더 멀리, 수백 µm까지
COMMOT — 거리 제한을 건 optimal transport. Ligand와 receptor가 서로를 두고 경쟁
CellChat v2 — spatial mode, contact 신호와 분비 신호의 범위를 따로 설정
LIANA+ — local score: 절편 어디에서 ligand와 receptor가 같이 높은가?
✅ Structure-preserving null과 비교(§2.2) — 예: receiver 층 전체를 통째로 이동. 가깝다는 건 조직 구조로 예상되는 것보다 더 가까울 때만 의미 있음
⚠️ 여전히 mRNA 옆의 mRNA: protein x, 결합 x, 반응 x. W6 가설이 올라가 봤자 ③단계 (🔗 §3)
⚠️ Visium에선 sender와 receiver가 spot 하나를 공유할 수 있음 → “가깝다”의 기준이 biology가 아니라 55 µm. Single-cell platform이 더 깔끔한 버전 — 단, §1.4의 segmentation 주의점 그대로

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
section: 3) ⚠️ Label-free vs TMT — when the plex is the batch
text:
3) ⚠️ Label-free vs TMT — when the plex is the batch



TMT runs 16–18 samples as one. That one run is also one batch.



Label-free — every sample is its own LC-MS run (DDA or DIA). ✅ No limit on the number of samples. ⚠️ Run order and instrument drift become the batch
TMT (isobaric labelling) — tag each sample’s peptides with a different mass tag, pool 16–18 samples, run once. The tags separate only after fragmentation (reporter ions)

✅ Within a plex, every sample is measured on the same peptides → the missing-value problem moves from “per sample” to “per plex”
⚠️ The plex is the batch. A cohort of 100 = 6–7 plexes; values compare well within a plex, much less across
⚠️ Ratio compression — co-isolated peptides pull every ratio towards 1 → fold changes are underestimated (MS3 or a narrower isolation window helps)

✅ For TMT: balance groups within every plex, and put the same pooled reference sample in every plex to bridge them

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
section: 3) From discovery to a clinical assay: targeted MS
text:
3) From discovery to a clinical assay: targeted MS



Each stage trades breadth for precision and sample number.


Discovery proteomics (DIA, TMT) measures thousands of proteins in tens of samples — and its output is a candidate list, not a test.

Targeted MS (PRM / MRM) — the instrument watches only chosen peptides → better precision and more samples per day, for fewer proteins
Heavy-isotope standards — spike in a known amount of the same peptide made with heavy isotopes. Light / heavy ratio × spiked amount = absolute concentration
✅ The protein is read as a digested peptide by mass → interfering autoantibodies are digested too, and an epitope change cannot hide it (the §4.1 problem). Your hospital lab already does this: thyroglobulin by LC-MS/MS when anti-Tg autoantibodies make the immunoassay unreliable
⚠️ Each stage needs a new, larger, independent cohort. Most discovery candidates never reach the last one (🔗 W10 §3)

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
section: 4) Proteins in place: tissue sections and single cells
text:
4) Proteins in place: tissue sections and single cells



The same antibodies on a slide — with the segmentation and epitope caveats attached.


The spatial logic of W7–W8, with proteins instead of RNA:

Multiplex IF (4–8 markers) → cyclic IF / CODEX (PhenoCycler) (40–100 markers; stain, image, strip, repeat) → IMC / MIBI (metal-tagged antibodies read by mass, ~40 markers)
✅ Works on FFPE (🔗 W7 §2.2), measures the effector molecule itself, and pathologists already read IHC
Analysis = W7–W8 again: segment → phenotype cells by marker intensity → neighbourhoods (🔗 W8 §2). The colorectal-cancer CODEX study that made “neighbourhood” a unit of analysis (Schürch 2020) is exactly this
⚠️ Still affinity — every marker is an antibody: validate each one in your tissue and fixation (the §4.1 problem on a slide)
⚠️ Still segmentation — membrane markers spill into neighbouring cells just like transcripts (🔗 W7 §3.2)
In suspension: CITE-seq reads antibody–oligo tags with the same cell barcode as the RNA (🔗 W5 §3.2) → protein and RNA from one cell

title: W9. 단백체학 — 단백질을 실제로 측정하는 방법
text:
3) ⚠️ Label-free vs TMT — plex = batch



TMT = sample 16–18개를 한 run으로. 그 한 run이 곧 batch 하나



Label-free — sample마다 LC-MS run 하나씩 (DDA든 DIA든). ✅ Sample 수 제한 x. ⚠️ Run 순서, 장비 drift가 batch
TMT (isobaric labelling) — sample마다 peptide에 서로 다른 mass tag → 16–18개를 섞어 한 번에 run. Tag는 fragment된 뒤에야 갈라짐 (reporter ion)

✅ 한 plex 안에선 모든 sample을 같은 peptide로 잼 → missing 문제가 “sample별”에서 “plex별”로 옮겨감
⚠️ Plex = batch. Cohort 100명 = plex 6–7개. Plex 안에선 비교가 잘 되지만, plex 사이는 훨씬 덜
⚠️ Ratio compression — 같이 분리된 다른 peptide가 모든 비율을 1 쪽으로 끌어당김 → fold change 과소추정 (MS3나 좁은 isolation window가 도움)

✅ TMT라면: plex마다 군을 균형 있게 배치 + 모든 plex에 같은 pooled reference sample을 넣어 plex끼리 연결

title: W9. 단백체학 — 단백질을 실제로 측정하는 방법
text:
3) Discovery에서 임상 assay까지: targeted MS



단계마다 범위를 내주고 정밀도와 sample 수를 얻음


Discovery proteomics(DIA, TMT) = sample 수십 개에서 protein 수천 개 → 결과물 = 후보 목록이지 검사가 아님

Targeted MS (PRM / MRM) — 장비가 미리 고른 peptide만 지켜봄 → 정밀도 ↑, 하루에 도는 sample 수 ↑, 대신 protein 수 ↓
Heavy-isotope 표준물질 — 같은 peptide를 무거운 동위원소로 만들어 정해진 양을 spike-in. Light / heavy 비율 × 넣은 양 = 절대 농도
✅ Protein을 분해된 peptide의 질량으로 읽음 → 방해하던 자가항체도 같이 분해되고, epitope가 바뀌어도 숨지 못함 (§4.1 문제). 병원 검사실이 이미 하는 방법: anti-Tg 자가항체 때문에 면역측정을 믿기 어려울 때 thyroglobulin을 LC-MS/MS로
⚠️ 단계마다 새롭고, 더 크고, 독립적인 cohort가 필요. Discovery 후보 대부분은 마지막 단계까지 못 감 (🔗 W10 §3)

title: W9. 단백체학 — 단백질을 실제로 측정하는 방법
section: 4) 제자리의 protein: 조직 절편과 single cell
text:
4) 제자리의 protein: 조직 절편과 single cell



같은 항체를 이번엔 slide 위에서. Segmentation과 epitope 주의점도 그대로 따라옴


W7–W8의 spatial 논리를 RNA 대신 protein으로:

Multiplex IF(marker 4–8개) → cyclic IF / CODEX(PhenoCycler)(40–100개, 염색–촬영–제거를 반복) → IMC / MIBI(금속 표지 항체를 질량으로 읽음, ~40개)
✅ FFPE에서 됨(🔗 W7 §2.2), 실제로 일하는 분자 자체를 잼, 병리의사는 이미 IHC를 읽음
분석 = W7–W8 그대로: segmentation → marker intensity로 cell phenotyping → neighbourhood (🔗 W8 §2). “Neighbourhood”를 분석 단위로 만든 대장암 CODEX 연구(Schürch 2020)가 정확히 이것
⚠️ 여전히 affinity — marker 하나하나가 항체: 내 조직, 내 고정 조건에서 항체마다 검증 (§4.1 문제의 slide 버전)
⚠️ 여전히 segmentation — membrane marker도 transcript처럼 이웃 cell로 번짐 (🔗 W7 §3.2)
Suspension에선: CITE-seq = 항체–oligo tag를 RNA와 같은 cell barcode로 읽음 (🔗 W5 §3.2) → 한 cell에서 protein + RNA
